items.subtype: Blank completion: phrase options (a/an + noun + preposition)
items.passage: Because parents who value self-reliance are inclined to give their children distinctive names, economists Samuel Bazzi, Martin Fiszbein, and Mesay Gebresilasse treated the prevalence of infrequent first names in a US county as ______ individualism there. As late as 1940, such names remained more common in counties with longer histories of frontier settlement.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A barometer of something is an indicator that registers how much of it is present. The text explains that “parents who value self-reliance are inclined to give their children distinctive names,” so the prevalence of infrequent names in a county rises with individualism there. That is why the economists could treat it as a barometer of individualism.

A.why_wrong: A repudiation of individualism would be a rejection of it. The text presents distinctive names as something chosen by parents who “value self-reliance,” so the names express individualism rather than reject it.

B.recipe: near miss: wrong direction of the relation (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: An impetus for individualism would be something that drives people toward it. The text runs the other way: parents who “value self-reliance” choose distinctive names, so the names reflect individualism that already exists rather than produce it.

D.why_wrong: A prerequisite for individualism would be something required before it could exist. Nothing in the text suggests that people need distinctive names in order to be individualistic; the names are only a sign of it.

sources.what: Boston University article on Bazzi, Fiszbein and Gebresilasse’s frontier study: individualistic types are prone to give their children infrequent names, reflecting a desire to stand out (a names-based measure borrowed from social psychologists); as late as 1940, families in long-established frontier counties favored unusual names; longer frontier exposure linked to individualism and opposition to redistribution

items.notes: Subject: social science (economic history). Key letter C. Band-7 moves: a familiar word in a transferred sense (barometer, a weather instrument, used for a social indicator); the clue is a cause clause (Because ... distinctive names) one level more abstract than the key, so the student must see that a choice driven by self-reliance can serve as a gauge of it; near miss an impetus for fails only on the direction of the relation. Steps: 2. Raw freq.txt ranks (reviewer): a repudiation of 20,957; an impetus for 15,727; a barometer of 17,917; a prerequisite for absent (all four past 10,000, two past 20,000). Key not the longest option.

fixes: replaced distractors a deterrent to and a catalyst for (wording copied from model 3021d9ef: deterrents to, catalysts of) with a repudiation of (reversal) and an impetus for (direction near miss); rewrote their why_wrong
dropped markedly from more common (the BU source says only that frontier counties chose more unusual names)

band7.why: after the distractor swap all four options past rank 10,000 (two past 20,000), key a transferred sense (barometer as social indicator), near miss impetus for fails only on direction; logic is two steps with a cause clause rather than the model's concessive frame, so it sits at the low end of band 7

items.passage: Although attitudes toward women’s work outside the home are often assumed to be ______ a country’s present economic conditions, economists Alberto Alesina, Paola Giuliano, and Nathan Nunn found that among second-generation immigrants raised in the United States, women whose parents came from cultures that traditionally farmed with the plough were less likely to be in the labor force.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Contingent on means depending on. The word “Although” sets the common assumption against the finding. The “second-generation immigrants raised in the United States” all grew up under the same present economic conditions, yet women whose parents came from “cultures that traditionally farmed with the plough were less likely to be in the labor force.” That challenges the assumption that such attitudes are contingent on present economic conditions, since inherited culture made a difference.

B.recipe: reversal: the trait of the finding, not of the challenged view (ANT)
B.why_wrong: Impervious to means unaffected by. The finding, that women of plough-farming descent worked less even under the same US conditions, fits the idea that attitudes can be unaffected by present conditions, so “Although” would set the finding against nothing; the assumption being challenged must be the opposite one.

C.recipe: near miss: wrong direction of the relation (CONNOT)
C.why_wrong: Conducive to means helping to bring about. The text is not about whether attitudes help the economy; the assumption it challenges is that economic conditions shape the attitudes, which the comparison among second-generation immigrants tests.

D.why_wrong: Antithetical to means directly opposed to. Nothing in the text suggests that anyone assumes attitudes toward women’s work are opposed to a country’s economic conditions; the question the study addresses is what those attitudes depend on.

sources.what: Alesina, Giuliano and Nunn, On the Origins of Gender Roles: Women and the Plough (IZA DP 5735, published QJE 2013): to separate culture from institutions and markets they examine second-generation immigrants in the US, who were all exposed to the same institutions and markets; women from cultures that historically used the plough have lower rates of labor force participation in the US

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Key letter A. Band-7 moves: concessive frame (Although ... often assumed) with the blank on the view being challenged, and the finding’s own trait (impervious to) offered as a reversal; the student must supply the unstated premise that second-generation immigrants raised in the US share the same present conditions (three steps: undo the concession, see the shared economy, see that ancestry still mattered). Raw freq.txt ranks: contingent on 17,762; impervious to 20,091; conducive to 24,104; antithetical to absent (all four past 10,000). Key not the longest option.

band7.why: concessive frame with the blank on the challenged view, the finding's own trait (impervious to) offered as the reversal, an unstated premise (US-raised children share present conditions) needed; all four options past rank 10,000, as in model 1455b754

items.passage: The anatomy of Daphnia lumholtzi, a tiny crustacean first detected in North American reservoirs in 1991 and since documented in more than a dozen US states, is remarkably ______. Individuals exposed to chemicals released by predators grow an enlarged helmet and a long tail spine, whereas those raised without such cues are morphologically similar to other Daphnia species.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Malleable means readily changed in form. The text shows the species taking two shapes depending on its surroundings: individuals “exposed to chemicals released by predators grow an enlarged helmet and a long tail spine,” whereas those “raised without such cues are morphologically similar to other Daphnia species.” Anatomy that changes in this way is malleable.

A.recipe: near miss: true of part of the clue (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: An enlarged helmet and long spine may be conspicuous, but the text’s point is the contrast between two forms: without such cues individuals “are morphologically similar to other Daphnia species,” so the species’ anatomy is not remarkable for being conspicuous.

B.why_wrong: Uniform means the same in every case. The text describes the opposite: individuals of this one species look quite different depending on whether they have detected predators.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions predators, but it never says this crustacean is especially vulnerable to them; it describes how the animal’s shape changes when it detects their chemicals.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Daphnia lumholtzi: a long tail spine, large helmet and additional spines are produced in response to predator kairomones; without them it looks morphologically similar to other Daphnia species; first detected in Missouri and Texas reservoirs in 1991; since spread to more than 16 states

items.notes: Subject: natural science (biology). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (compare the two conditions, then name the property they show). Band 6 by plan: plain key in the manner of variable (3.4) and homogeneous (3.8), with the clue in the next sentence; the near miss conspicuous is true of the predator-induced form but not of the species as the text presents it. Raw freq.txt ranks: conspicuous 6,466; uniform 4,122; vulnerable 23,199; malleable 51,674. Key not the longest option. Kairomones simplified to chemicals given off by predators.

fixes: virtually identical to other Daphnia species changed to are morphologically similar to other Daphnia species (the source's wording: looks morphologically similar); explanation and why_wrong A requoted
since recorded in changed to since documented in (keeps the hard tier's long-word share at CB's level after the change above); why_wrong A its anatomy made the species’ anatomy

band7.why: band 6 by plan: plain key (malleable) from a two-condition comparison as in 3.4 variable; near miss conspicuous true of one form only

items.passage: Most people consider calming down the best way to handle nerves before a stressful performance. Psychologist Alison Wood Brooks found, however, that performers need not ______ their anxiety to succeed: participants who reappraised their anxiety as excitement, sometimes just by saying “I am excited” aloud, outperformed those who tried to relax.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To subdue a feeling is to bring it under control or quiet it. The text sets the common view of “calming down” as “the best way to handle nerves” against Brooks’s finding: participants “who reappraised their anxiety as excitement” outperformed “those who tried to relax.” Anxious performers therefore need not subdue their anxiety; relabeling it works better than quieting it.

A.why_wrong: To harness anxiety is to put it to use, which is what reappraising it as excitement does. Saying performers “need not” harness it would contradict the finding that those who reappraised their anxiety did better.

C.why_wrong: The text never discusses whether performers reveal their anxiety to others; saying “I am excited” relabels the feeling rather than disclosing anxiety.

D.why_wrong: Performers may anticipate a stressful task, but the text says nothing about whether they must anticipate their anxiety; it compares relabeling anxiety with trying to calm it.

sources.what: Brooks 2014, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, Get excited: reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 24364682): most people believe trying to calm down is the best way to cope; compared with those who attempt to calm down, individuals who reappraise anxious arousal as excitement perform better; saying “I am excited” out loud; karaoke singing, public speaking and math

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (undo need not, then see that the finding favors relabeling over quieting). Band 6 by plan: the negation is stated outright and the reversal harness is the natural positive word under need not, as in the band-6 negated models. Raw freq.txt ranks: harness 7,347; subdue 15,435; disclose 12,686; anticipate 10,355. Key not the longest option.

band7.why: band 6 by plan: negation stated outright (need not), reversal harness is the natural positive word, key requires undoing the negation and reading the finding as relabel over calm

items.passage:
The following text is from Henry James’s 1878 novel The Europeans. Felix has just told his cousin Gertrude that her sister, who is walking in the distance with a young minister, Mr. Brand, seems to enjoy his company.

And in the excitement of observation Felix rose to his feet.

Gertrude rose also, but she made no attempt to emulate her companion’s discovery; she looked rather in another direction. Felix’s words had struck her; but a certain delicacy <u>checked</u> her. “She is certainly not indifferent to Mr. Brand; she has the highest opinion of him.”
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “checked” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “checked” means curbed, or held back. Felix stands up in “the excitement of observation,” and Gertrude, though she “rose also,” “made no attempt to emulate her companion’s discovery” and “looked rather in another direction.” The sentence sets her delicacy, or sense of tact, against the pull of Felix’s words (“Felix’s words had struck her; but”), so her delicacy curbed her from staring at the couple as he did.

A.why_wrong: To check something can mean to scrutinize it, or examine it closely, but Gertrude’s delicacy does not examine her; it keeps her from looking, which is why she “looked rather in another direction.”

B.why_wrong: To check a fact can mean to corroborate, or confirm, it, but nothing is being confirmed in this sentence; Gertrude’s delicacy acts on her, keeping her from following Felix’s gaze.

D.why_wrong: Felix’s words “had struck her,” so Gertrude may be unsettled, but “but” sets her delicacy against that effect; what the delicacy does is hold her back, as her looking “in another direction” shows, not disconcert her.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg #179, Henry James, The Europeans (1878): last sentence of the paragraph in which Felix rises to watch Charlotte and Mr. Brand, and the following paragraph, copied exactly (the dialogue before them summarized in the intro line)

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1878). Key letter C. Band-7 moves: a common target (checked) in a sense that is not its first one; the key is a mid-frequency word rather than the plain synonym (stopped); two distractors are real senses of check (scrutinize, corroborate) and one is a scene word built from struck her; the clue words are themselves less common or used in secondary senses (delicacy as tact, emulate). Raw freq.txt ranks: Scrutinized 18,297; Corroborated 22,317; Curbed 26,637; Disconcerted 8,436 (three of four past 10,000). Key not the longest option. The Europeans is used in no official item of any skill and in none of ours; Henry James appears in no official transcript.

band7.why: Wharton/Beckett pattern: common target in a secondary sense, mid-frequency key (Curbed) rather than stopped, two real senses of check (scrutinize, corroborate) and a scene word (Disconcerted); three of four options past rank 10,000; the real-sense distractors fit the slot only loosely, as Situated and Realized do in 7f935017

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Literary scholar Myriam Chancy has suggested that the family of Haitian novelist Marie Vieux-Chauvet bought back unsold copies of her 1968 trilogy Amour, colère et folie because they regarded it as ______, since its depictions of civilians menaced by soldiers and paramilitary forces could be interpreted as criticism of François Duvalier’s regime and so invite reprisals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Incendiary describes something likely to stir up anger or conflict, as if it could start a fire. According to the text, the trilogy’s depictions “could be interpreted as criticism of François Duvalier’s regime and so invite reprisals.” A book that might provoke a dangerous response from the government is one the family would regard as incendiary.

B.recipe: near miss: same evaluative family, wrong ground (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: Lurid means shocking in a sensational way. Depictions of “civilians menaced by soldiers” might be disturbing, but the reason the text gives for buying back copies is political danger (criticism of the regime that could “invite reprisals”), not sensationalism.

C.why_wrong: Anodyne means harmless and unlikely to offend. A book that could be interpreted as criticism of Duvalier’s regime and invite reprisals is the opposite of anodyne.

D.why_wrong: Abstruse means hard to understand. The text says nothing about the trilogy being difficult; the family’s worry was that readers could take it as criticism of the government.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Marie Vieux-Chauvet: Amour, Colère et Folie (1968, Gallimard) suppressed and withdrawn from circulation for unclear reasons; Myriam J. A. Chancy suggests the family feared government reprisal due to the trilogy’s criticism of the Duvalier regime and suppressed distribution by buying back unsold copies; in Colère a military commander confiscates a family’s land, in Folie poets are trapped by local paramilitary forces

items.notes: Subject: humanities (literary history). Key letter A. Band-7 moves: B2 with the cause in a since clause in the same sentence (one sentence, as in the band-7 B2 models) and an evaluative key in a transferred sense (incendiary, literally fire-starting); near miss lurid comes from the same family of words for disturbing books but fails on the ground the text gives; the rest are rare. Steps: 2 (from feared reprisals to the book’s quality). Raw freq.txt ranks: incendiary 32,026; lurid 8,766; anodyne 30,763; abstruse 24,252 (three past 20,000). The passage attributes the account to Chancy, as the source does, since other accounts of the withdrawal differ. Key is the longest option.

band7.why: B2 with the cause in a since clause in one sentence as in 571cf537 and a756aa95; evaluative key in a transferred sense, near miss lurid from the same family with the wrong ground; three options past rank 20,000

items.passage: Ahuna Mons, a mountain about 4 kilometers tall, is the only obvious cryovolcano, or ice volcano, on the dwarf planet Ceres. Planetary scientist Michael Sori and colleagues propose that it is unlikely to have been ______, however: older cryovolcanoes may have flattened over hundreds of millions of years, as ice slowly flows, until they became indistinguishable from the surrounding terrain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Something unprecedented has never happened before. Sori’s team proposes that Ahuna Mons only looks alone: “older cryovolcanoes may have flattened over hundreds of millions of years” until they “became indistinguishable from the surrounding terrain.” If such volcanoes existed earlier, Ahuna Mons is unlikely to have been unprecedented.

A.why_wrong: Ahuna Mons is described as “the only obvious cryovolcano” on Ceres, so it is conspicuous; saying it is unlikely to have been conspicuous contradicts the first sentence.

B.why_wrong: The text never discusses whether Ahuna Mons is still active or dormant; its argument is about older ice volcanoes that have flattened out of sight.

C.recipe: near miss: the trait of the older volcanoes (CONNOT)
C.why_wrong: Ephemeral means short-lived. The text suggests that ice volcanoes on Ceres do not last as visible features, since older ones “flattened,” so it gives no reason to deny that Ahuna Mons is ephemeral too; the point of “however” is that it was not the first.

sources.what: USGS publication page, Sori et al. 2017, The vanishing cryovolcanoes of Ceres (Geophysical Research Letters): Ahuna Mons is a 4 km tall mountain on Ceres interpreted as a geologically young cryovolcanic dome; other cryovolcanic features are less clear, so either cryovolcanism is recent or older structures have been altered beyond recognition; the authors test whether domes viscously relax (AGU release: older cryovolcanoes may have flattened out and become indistinguishable from the surface, as glaciers flow)

items.notes: Subject: natural science (planetary science). Key letter D. Negated frame (unlikely to have been) as in the medium B5 models; the reversal conspicuous is the natural word for the only obvious volcano, and the near miss ephemeral describes the older volcanoes’ fate. Steps: 2. Raw freq.txt ranks: conspicuous 6,466; dormant 16,629; ephemeral 21,660; unprecedented 14,344. Key is the longest option.

items.passage: Sociologist Annette Lareau found that many middle-class parents in the United States practiced what she called “concerted cultivation,” enrolling their children in organized activities meant to develop their talents. Children raised this way tended to be ______ adults in positions of authority: they came to see such adults almost as equals and grew comfortable questioning them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be unintimidated by someone is to feel no fear or awe of that person. The text explains that these children “came to see such adults almost as equals and grew comfortable questioning them,” which is how people behave toward authorities who do not intimidate them.

A.why_wrong: Deferential to means respectfully yielding to. Children who “grew comfortable questioning” adults in authority and saw them “almost as equals” were the opposite of deferential.

C.recipe: near miss: wrong attitude behind the behavior (CONNOT)
C.why_wrong: Questioning adults might suggest resentment, but the text presents it as ease, not hostility: the children saw such adults “almost as equals” and were “comfortable” questioning them.

D.why_wrong: Children who regularly question adults in authority are engaged with them, not indifferent to them; nothing in the text suggests they did not care about such adults.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Concerted cultivation: Annette Lareau, Unequal Childhoods (2003); middle-class parents engage in concerted cultivation by attempting to foster children’s talents through organized activities; it encourages children to see adults as their equals, and children become more comfortable questioning adults

items.notes: Subject: social science (sociology). Key letter B. Restatement after a colon; one reversal, one near miss (resentful of) and one unsupported word, as the report gives for medium. Raw freq.txt ranks: deferential to 12,560; unintimidated by absent; resentful of 10,661; indifferent to 2,479. Key is the longest option.

items.passage: Armenian priest and musicologist Komitas was a remarkably ______ collector of folk music: spending summer after summer in villages of the Armenian countryside, where he built close relationships with the villagers, he transcribed more than 3,000 songs, though more than half of those transcriptions were later lost.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A prolific collector gathers a great many things. The text supports this description: Komitas spent “summer after summer in villages of the Armenian countryside” and “transcribed more than 3,000 songs.”

B.recipe: near miss: built from half of the clue (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: The text says that “more than half of those transcriptions were later lost,” but it does not blame Komitas for the loss; nothing suggests he was negligent, or careless, in his collecting.

C.why_wrong: A reluctant collector would be unwilling to do the work, but Komitas returned “summer after summer” and transcribed thousands of songs.

D.why_wrong: Unscrupulous means lacking moral principles. The text describes Komitas building “close relationships with the villagers,” and nothing suggests he collected songs dishonestly.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Komitas: Armenian priest and musicologist; spent summers in the Armenian countryside, building a unique relationship with villagers to gather songs; collected and transcribed over 3,000 pieces of Armenian folk music, more than half of which were subsequently lost (around 1,200 extant)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (music). Key letter A. Restatement after a colon; the near miss negligent is built from the later clause about lost transcriptions, which does not say who lost them. Raw freq.txt ranks: prolific 23,160; negligent 25,831; reluctant 6,398; unscrupulous 10,758. Key not the longest option.

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos Islands are threatened by an introduced parasitic fly, Philornis downsi. Because the finches readily collect soft fibers to line their nests, biologist Sarah Knutie and colleagues induced the birds to ______ their own nests: nests containing at least a gram of cotton treated with the insecticide permethrin were virtually parasite-free.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To fumigate a place is to treat it with a chemical that kills pests. Because the finches “readily collect soft fibers to line their nests,” they carried cotton “treated with the insecticide permethrin” into their nests, and those nests “were virtually parasite-free.” The birds were, in effect, fumigating their own nests.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about birds leaving their nests; it describes them adding treated cotton to nests that then became “virtually parasite-free.”

B.recipe: near miss: true of the material, not of its purpose (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: Soft cotton might insulate a nest, but the result the text reports is about the insecticide: nests with treated cotton “were virtually parasite-free,” not warmer.

D.why_wrong: To infest a nest would be to fill it with pests, which is the opposite of what happened: the treated nests were nearly free of the parasitic fly.

sources.what: Knutie, McNew, Bartlow, Vargas and Clayton 2014, Current Biology, Darwin’s finches combat introduced nest parasites with fumigated cotton (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 24801182): introduced nest fly Philornis downsi threatens Darwin’s finches; finches can be encouraged to self-fumigate nests with permethrin-treated cotton fibers; nests containing at least one gram of cotton were virtually parasite-free

items.notes: Subject: natural science (biology). Key letter C. Cause clause (Because the finches readily collect soft fibers) plus the consequence after the colon; the near miss insulate is what cotton does in a nest, but not what the result shows. The key is the paper’s own term (self-fumigate). Raw freq.txt ranks: abandon 5,885; insulate absent; fumigate absent; infest 39,719. Key tied for longest with insulate.

items.passage:
The following text is from George Gissing’s 1893 novel The Odd Women. Dr. Madden has just made a joke rather than answer a young guest, Rhoda Nunn, who asked him whether women should sit in Parliament.

[Dr. Madden’s] daughters would not have ventured to express an opinion on such topics when he was present; apart with Miss Nunn, they <u>betrayed</u> a timid interest in whatever proposition she advanced, but no gleam of originality distinguished their arguments.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “betrayed” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “betrayed” means revealed. In front of their father the daughters “would not have ventured to express an opinion” on topics such as women in Parliament, but “apart with Miss Nunn” they let a “timid interest in whatever proposition she advanced” show. They revealed that interest; nothing suggests disloyalty or deceit.

A.why_wrong: To betray someone can mean to deceive that person, but the daughters are not deceiving anyone by showing “a timid interest” in Rhoda’s ideas; the sentence is about what they let show when alone with her.

B.why_wrong: To betray a friend or cause can mean to abandon it, but the daughters do not abandon their interest; they show it, if timidly, when “apart with Miss Nunn.”

C.why_wrong: To betray someone can mean to report that person to an authority, but the daughters are not reporting anything to anyone; they simply show interest in Rhoda’s propositions.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg #4313, George Gissing, The Odd Women (1893), chapter 1: Dr. Madden answers Rhoda’s question about women in Parliament with a joke; the paragraph that follows copied exactly from its second sentence, with [Dr. Madden’s] replacing His

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1893). Key letter D. Abstract sense of an everyday word (betray as show unintentionally), with three distractors that are other senses of betray, as in 2.19 (assumed: Acquired, Acknowledged, Imitated, Speculated). Raw freq.txt ranks: Deceived 3,195; Abandoned 3,393; Reported 3,758; Revealed 2,383. Key not the longest option. The Odd Women is used in no official item of any skill and in none of ours.

items.passage: Norwegian painter Harriet Backer was a ______ artist. She worked slowly and methodically, completing only about 180 works throughout her long career, and she is best known for detailed interior scenes rendered in rich colors, with careful attention to the interplay of light and shadow.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A painstaking artist works with great care and effort. The next sentence says that Backer “worked slowly and methodically” and painted “detailed interior scenes” with “careful attention to the interplay of light and shadow,” which describes a painstaking artist.

A.why_wrong: A hasty artist works too quickly, but Backer “worked slowly and methodically.”

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about Backer rebelling against other artists or traditions; it describes how carefully she worked.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no sign that Backer has been forgotten; it says what she “is best known for.”

sources.what: Wikipedia, Harriet Backer: Norwegian painter best known for detailed interior scenes communicated with rich colors and the interplay of light and shadow; her work was both slow and thorough; produced just around 180 works

items.notes: Subject: humanities (painting). Key letter B. Restatement in the next sentence (slowly and methodically, careful attention). The source’s slow and thorough is paraphrased. Raw freq.txt ranks: hasty 3,745; painstaking 22,230; rebellious 9,434; forgotten 799. Key is the longest option.

items.passage: In 1897, Swedish explorer Salomon August Andrée and two companions attempted to reach the North Pole by hydrogen balloon, but their leaking balloon descended onto the pack ice after two days. For 33 years, the expedition’s fate remained ______: no one knew what had become of the explorers until a Norwegian expedition discovered their final camp on Kvitøya in 1930.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Something unresolved has not been settled or explained. The text says that “no one knew what had become of the explorers” until “a Norwegian expedition discovered their final camp on Kvitøya in 1930,” so the expedition’s fate remained unresolved for 33 years.

A.why_wrong: The text does not say the expedition’s fate was celebrated; it says “no one knew what had become of the explorers.”

B.why_wrong: A documented fate would be one recorded and known, but for 33 years “no one knew what had become of the explorers.”

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that anyone exaggerated what happened to the explorers; their fate was simply unknown.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Andrée’s Arctic balloon expedition: 1897 attempt to reach the North Pole by hydrogen balloon; the balloon lost hydrogen quickly and crashed on the pack ice after only two days; the Bratvaag expedition found the remains on Kvitøya on 5 August 1930, the chance discovery of the expedition’s last camp

items.notes: Subject: history (polar exploration). Key letter C. Restatement after a colon. Raw freq.txt ranks: celebrated 5,437; documented 5,158; unresolved 58,607; exaggerated 6,194. Key not the longest option.

items.passage: In 2017, paleoanthropologist Jean-Jacques Hublin and colleagues reported that fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, belong to Homo sapiens and are roughly 300,000 years old, making them the oldest known remains of our species. The fossils’ faces are strikingly ______: they closely resemble the faces of people living today, though the braincases are more elongated.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Modern means like the present day. The text explains that the fossils’ faces “closely resemble the faces of people living today,” so they look strikingly modern even though the fossils are about 300,000 years old.

B.why_wrong: The fossils are old, but the colon introduces how the faces look: they “closely resemble the faces of people living today,” which is the opposite of looking ancient.

C.why_wrong: Fossils can be fragile, but the text says nothing about their condition; it compares the faces with those of “people living today.”

D.why_wrong: Weathered suits old fossils, but the text describes what the faces resemble, not how worn they are.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Jebel Irhoud: Hublin et al. 2017 dated the remains to about 315,000 years ago, by far the earliest known examples of Homo sapiens; the facial features resemble modern H. sapiens, while the braincase has an elongated shape

items.notes: Subject: natural science (paleoanthropology). Key letter A. Restatement after a colon. 315,000 years rounded to roughly 300,000, as the 2017 reports did. Raw freq.txt ranks: modern 1,577; ancient 1,340; fragile 9,404; weathered 26,572. Key not the longest option.

The following text is adapted from Dorothy Canfield’s 1912 novel The Squirrel-Cage. Lydia is being fitted for a dress by Madame Boyle, a dressmaker, in a room crowded with chattering guests.

Mrs. Sandworth, her eyes full of tears, opened her arms impulsively, but Lydia drew back. “Oh, let me alone!” she wailed. “I’m so tired!”

Madame Boyle <u>caught</u> this through the clatter of voices. “Why, poor Maddemwaselle!” she cried, her kindly, harassed, fatigued face melting. “Sit down. Sit down.”
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “caught” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “caught” means heard. Madame Boyle picks out Lydia’s cry, “I’m so tired!”, “through the clatter of voices” in the crowded room and answers it at once, telling Lydia to “Sit down.” She heard what Lydia said.

A.why_wrong: To catch something can mean to grab it with the hands, but Lydia’s cry is not an object; Madame Boyle takes it in “through the clatter of voices.”

C.why_wrong: To catch an animal can mean to trap it, but nothing is trapped here; Madame Boyle simply responds to words she has picked out in the noise.

D.why_wrong: To catch a train or bus means to board it, but the text describes a dressmaker reacting to what Lydia says, not getting on any vehicle.

Sit down.”

The following text is from Ellen Glasgow’s 1904 novel The Deliverance. Christopher Blake has found his sister Cynthia ironing late at night.

“I had a little ironing to do,” she answered, “and I wanted it all finished to-night. Mother needs me in the day.”

Pushing her aside, he seized the iron and <u>ran</u> it in a few hasty strokes over the rough-dry garment which she had spread on the board. “Go to bed and leave these things alone,” he insisted.

“Oh, Christopher, you’ll spoil it!” cried Cynthia, clutching his arm.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “ran” most nearly mean?

A.why_wrong: To run a business means to manage it, but Christopher is not managing the iron; he pushes it “in a few hasty strokes over the rough-dry garment.”

B.why_wrong: A newspaper can run, or print, a story, but nothing is printed here; the text describes ironing a garment.

D.why_wrong: To run a horse in a race can mean to enter it, but the iron is not entered in anything; it travels across the garment on the board.

items.passage: Around 764, Japan’s Empress Shōtoku commissioned one million miniature wooden pagodas, each containing a brief Buddhist incantation printed on paper, an enormous undertaking that took about six years to complete. The pagodas were then ______ temples across the country, and today more than 45,000 of them survive at just one of those temples, Hōryū-ji, near Nara.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be distributed among a group is to be handed out to its members. The text says the pagodas went to “temples across the country” and that thousands now survive at “just one of those temples,” so they must have been distributed among many temples.

A.why_wrong: The empress had the pagodas made; they were not borrowed from temples but sent out to them, which is why some survive at “one of those temples.”

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says the pagodas were hidden under temples; it says they survive at a temple, Hōryū-ji.

C.why_wrong: The text gives no reason to think the pagodas were compared with temples; it describes where they were sent and where they survive.

items.passage: Wolverines are ______ snow for successful reproduction: each February, a female excavates a den within the snowpack, and her offspring remain there until they are weaned in mid-May. Consequently, wolverines live year-round only in regions where snow cover persists into late spring.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

The text explains that a female wolverine “excavates a den within the snowpack,” where her offspring remain “until they are weaned in mid-May,” and that wolverines therefore “live year-round only in regions where snow cover persists into late spring.” They are dependent on snow.

B.why_wrong: Wolverines are not frightened of snow; females deliberately dig their dens in it, and the animals live only where it persists into spring.

C.why_wrong: Animals that dig dens in the snowpack and live only where snow persists are hardly unaware of it.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about wolverines’ fame; it explains why they need snow for successful reproduction.

items.passage: Because sociologist Mitchell Duneier spent months working at the tables of vendors who sold used books and magazines along New York City’s Sixth Avenue, his 1999 book Sidewalk offers a ______ account of their lives. It describes, from his own observation, how the sidewalk gave the vendors income, respect, and social support.

items.explanation: A firsthand account comes from the writer’s own direct experience. Because Duneier “spent months working at the tables” of the vendors, his book describes their lives “from his own observation,” which makes it a firsthand account.

A.why_wrong: The text presents Sidewalk as a sociologist’s study based on “his own observation,” not as an invented story.

B.why_wrong: A secondhand account relies on what others report, but Duneier worked beside the vendors himself and wrote “from his own observation.” The vendors sold used books, but the account is not secondhand.

items.passage: The Czech painter born Marie Čermínová adopted the name Toyen in 1923, possibly derived from the French word citoyen, meaning “citizen.” The pseudonym does not ______ its bearer’s gender, which suited an artist who, according to the poet Vítězslav Nezval, refused to use feminine grammatical endings when speaking Czech.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To reveal something is to make it known. The name Toyen gives no clue whether its bearer is a woman or a man, which “suited an artist who” “refused to use feminine grammatical endings.” So the pseudonym does not reveal its bearer’s gender.

B.why_wrong: A name that keeps gender hidden does disguise it; saying it “does not” disguise its bearer’s gender would mean the name shows it, which would not suit an artist who avoided feminine grammatical endings.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions a French word, but a name cannot translate a person’s gender; the point is whether the name shows it.

D.why_wrong: A name may be short, but it makes no sense to say a name shortens someone’s gender; the text is about whether the name shows gender.

A.why_wrong: A sluggish traveler moves slowly, but this fox covered “3,506 kilometers in only 76 days.”

items.passage: A local church tax in Germany had long gone unenforced, so economist Nadja Dwenger and colleagues treated the sizable payments members made anyway as intrinsically motivated. When the researchers then warned some members of enforcement or offered others rewards for paying, that voluntary compliance did not decline, suggesting that such incentives are ______ intrinsic motivation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: When the researchers added warnings and rewards, “that voluntary compliance did not decline.” The incentives worked alongside what members already paid of their own accord instead of pushing that motive aside, so the two kinds of motivation can exist together: the incentives are compatible with intrinsic motivation.

A.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that the incentives depend on intrinsic motivation; the text describes the incentives and the voluntary compliance existing side by side.

B.why_wrong: If the incentives were a substitute for intrinsic motivation, they would take its place and voluntary compliance would fall, but the text says that compliance “did not decline.”

D.why_wrong: A catalyst for intrinsic motivation would make it grow, but the text says only that voluntary compliance “did not decline,” not that the warnings and rewards increased it.

sources.what: Dwenger, Kleven, Rasul, Rincke, AEJ: Economic Policy 8(3) 2016, abstract: German local church tax historically relied on zero deterrence, so baseline compliance is intrinsically motivated; field experiment incentivized compliance through deterrence or rewards; intrinsic compliance is substantial, driven partly by duty-to-comply preferences; no crowd-out between extrinsic and intrinsic motivations (abstract read via the OpenAlex record of this DOI)

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral public finance). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (incentives were added and voluntary compliance did not fall, so the two motives coexist; then the relation word). Ranks (freq.txt, rarest content word): contingent 17,762; substitute 9,221; compatible 23,068; catalyst not listed. Near miss: a catalyst for (the text says only that voluntary compliance did not decline, not that it grew). Treatments simplified to rewards or warnings of enforcement; the passage does not say how members were contacted.

review.note: Core claim (zero-deterrence church tax, deterrence or reward treatments, no crowd-out) checked on the AEA abstract page.

Two steps (incentives added, voluntary compliance unchanged, so the motives coexist), key paraphrased away from the passage, catalyst for a near miss that fails on one feature (growth vs no loss).

items.subtype: Blank completion: phrase options (a/an + noun + preposition)
items.passage: For years, variations in the oxygen isotope ratios of stalagmites from Chinese caves were widely interpreted as ______ the quantity of rain delivered by the East Asian summer monsoon. Geoscientists Barbara Maher and Roy Thompson challenged that interpretation in 2012, arguing that the variations reflect shifts in the source of the moisture rather than changes in the amount of precipitation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Maher and Thompson “challenged that interpretation,” arguing that the variations reflect “shifts in the source of the moisture rather than changes in the amount of precipitation.” The interpretation they challenged must therefore have tied the variations to the amount of rain, treating them as a measure, or gauge, of “the quantity of rain delivered by the East Asian summer monsoon.”

B.recipe: reversal: trait of the wrong party (ANT)
B.why_wrong: Treating the variations as independent of the amount of rain is Maher and Thompson’s position, not the earlier interpretation they “challenged.”

C.why_wrong: Isotope ratios in cave formations could not have produced the monsoon’s rain; the earlier reading treated the ratios as recording rainfall, not causing it.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that anyone thought the variations held back how much rain fell; the dispute is over what the isotope record measures.

sources.what: Maher, Thompson, Journal of Quaternary Science 27 (2012), abstract: oxygen isotope variations in Chinese stalagmites have been widely interpreted as a record of the amount of East Asian summer monsoonal rainfall; the variations cannot be accounted for by summer rainfall changes but instead reflect changes in moisture source

items.notes: Subject: natural science (paleoclimatology). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (the blank is the received view; the challenge says rather than the amount of rainfall, so the received view treated the ratios as measuring it). Band-7 B3 move used: blank on the view being challenged, with the challengers' trait (independent of) as a reversal. Ranks: gauge 16,357; independent 3,829; cause 715; hindrance 14,036. A constraint on was replaced in review: in geoscience usage a proxy that provides a constraint on rainfall measures it, a second reading close to the key.

fixes: option D a constraint on replaced by a hindrance to: 'a constraint on' has a technical sense (data that puts bounds on an estimate) that a science-literate student could read as a measure of rainfall, close to the key; why_wrong D and notes updated
review.note: Core claim (stalagmite oxygen isotopes widely read as monsoon rainfall amount; Maher and Thompson 2012 argue moisture source instead) checked on the OpenAlex abstract of the DOI.

band7.why: Target 6 by plan. Raw ranks a gauge of 16,357; independent of 3,829; a cause of 715; a hindrance to 14,036: 2 of 4 past 10,000. items.passage: Legal historian Emily Kadens argues that the story of a medieval “law merchant,” a body of commercial law supposedly created and enforced by merchants themselves, has an unusually ______ hold on scholars interested in private ordering. Although numerous historical studies have demonstrated its falsity, the story still appears regularly in scholarship as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The text says that “numerous historical studies have demonstrated its falsity,” yet “the story still appears regularly in scholarship as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce.” A belief that keeps its grip on scholars even after repeated refutation has a persistent, stubborn hold, so the hold is tenacious.

A.why_wrong: A precarious hold would be insecure and likely to slip, as one might expect of a story whose “falsity” numerous studies have demonstrated, but the story “still appears regularly in scholarship as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce,” so its hold has stayed firm.

B.why_wrong: Apocryphal means of doubtful truth. It describes the story itself, whose “falsity” studies have demonstrated, not the hold the story has on scholars, who still present it “as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce.”

C.why_wrong: Equivocal means uncertain or ambiguous, but the story still appears in scholarship “as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce,” which shows a firm rather than an uncertain hold.

sources.what: Kadens, The Medieval Law Merchant: The Tyranny of a Construct, Journal of Legal Analysis 7 (2015), abstract: the story of a medieval law merchant has a strong hold on scholars interested in private ordering; despite numerous historical works demonstrating the falsity of the myth, it continues to be discussed regularly in scholarship as if it were an accurate portrayal of the past

items.notes: Subject: history and social science (legal history). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (refuted yet still treated as accurate, so the hold persists; then the trait word). Ranks: precarious 13,764; apocryphal 39,430; equivocal 24,700; tenacious 15,769. The gloss of the law merchant (law made and enforced by traders) is the standard description of the construct Kadens tests. Review: ephemeral replaced by precarious so that a wrong option also collocates with hold (precarious hold) and is the reading the concessive half invites.
band7_moves: all four options past rank 10,000, two past 20,000
clue phrased in a different register from the key (still appears in scholarship although its falsity has been demonstrated)
topic-echo trap that describes the myth rather than its hold (apocryphal)
collocating reversal built from the concessive half (precarious hold), added in review

fixes: option A ephemeral replaced by precarious: only the key collocated with hold (tenacious hold), so the item solved by collocation; precarious hold is a stock phrase and the trap the concessive 'Although ... falsity' half invites; why_wrong A and notes updated
review.note: Core claim (law merchant story keeps a strong hold on private-ordering scholars despite works showing it false) checked on the OpenAlex abstract of the DOI.

band7.why: After the fix: raw ranks precarious 13,764; apocryphal 39,430; equivocal 24,700; tenacious 15,769: 4 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 4.33. Concessive frame ('Although ... demonstrated its falsity, ... still appears'), two collocating options (tenacious hold, precarious hold) with the reversal built from the concessive half, and apocryphal names the passage's 'falsity' but describes the story, not its hold.

items.passage: Analyzing extensive supermarket scanner data and online prices, economist Daniel Levy and colleagues found that 9 is the most common final digit and that prices ending in 9 are less ______ than other prices. Such prices tend to persist for longer intervals, and the most frequent revisions are ones that preserve the 9 ending.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Prices ending in 9 “tend to persist for longer intervals,” and even when they are revised, “the most frequent revisions are ones that preserve the 9 ending.” Such prices resist change, so they are less mutable, or less likely to change, than other prices.

A.why_wrong: Remunerative means profitable. The sentence that follows the blank gives evidence about how rarely the prices change, not about how much money they bring in.

C.why_wrong: Sacrosanct means too important to be changed. Prices that hold longer and keep their 9 when revised are more sacrosanct than others, not less.

D.why_wrong: Ostentatious means showy. Nothing in the text concerns how prices ending in 9 display themselves; it reports how seldom they change.

sources.what: Levy, Lee, Chen, Kauffman, Bergen, Price Points and Price Rigidity, Review of Economics and Statistics 93(4) 2011, abstract: weekly scanner data and Internet data; 9 is the most frequent ending; the most common price changes keep the price endings at 9; 9-ending prices are less likely to change than non-9-ending prices; 9-ending contributes to price rigidity

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics of pricing). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (less + mutable; the evidence shows prices that resist change). Ranks: remunerative 31,748; mutable 50,138; sacrosanct not listed; ostentatious 20,698. Not the left-digit bias (live in two items): this is how often prices change. The abstract's result on the size of price changes is left out.

reversal of the implied logic (sacrosanct) instead of a negation flip

review.note: Core claim (9 the commonest ending, 9-ending prices less likely to change, changes keep the 9) checked on the OpenAlex abstract.

band7.why: Raw ranks remunerative 31,748; mutable 50,138; sacrosanct unseen; ostentatious 20,698: 4 of 4 past 20,000, key past 50,000, rarest distractor unseen. items.passage:
The following text is from Owen Wister’s 1906 novel Lady Baltimore. The narrator is talking with Miss La Heu, whose dog, General, was recently killed by an automobile.

“Oh, his heart! General, listen to—” From habit she had turned to where her dog used to lie; and sudden pain swept over her face and was <u>mastered</u>. “Never mind!” she quickly resumed. “Please don’t speak about it. And you have a heart somewhere; for it was very nice in you to come in yesterday morning after—after the bridge.”
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “mastered” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Miss La Heu turns by habit to her dead dog’s spot, and “sudden pain swept over her face.” Right after that she says “Never mind!” and “quickly resumed” the conversation, so the pain was brought under control. In this context “mastered” means subdued.

B.why_wrong: To master a skill or subject is to learn it, but Miss La Heu is not learning her pain; she is bringing it under control so that she can go on talking.

C.why_wrong: The pain did show when it “swept over her face,” but “mastered” describes what happened next, when she controlled it and “quickly resumed” speaking, not its being revealed.

D.why_wrong: To tolerate pain is only to put up with it. “Mastered” goes further: Miss La Heu brings the pain under control, and right away she “quickly resumed” with “Never mind!”

B.why_wrong: The examples are clothing and personal objects, not portraits; the people themselves do not appear in the photographs described.

Because members of the Mbeere dialect group seldom intermarry with the neighboring Chuka and Tharaka, researcher Vanesse Labeyrie and colleagues discovered, seed exchanges between the Mbeere and those communities are ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Seeds are mostly “exchanged among relatives,” and the Mbeere “seldom intermarry” with the Chuka and Tharaka, so few Mbeere farmers have relatives in those groups. As a result, seed exchanges between the Mbeere and those communities are limited.

A.why_wrong: Since seeds pass mainly between relatives and the groups “seldom intermarry,” exchanges between them would be rare, not frequent.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns whether the exchanges make money; it explains who exchanges seeds with whom.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no reason to think the exchanges are hidden; it explains why they are uncommon.

items.passage: A large log-jam repeatedly forms where Texas’s San Antonio River is shifting its course into a channel called Elm Bayou. Geographer Jonathan Phillips determined, however, that the jam did not ______ that shift. Instead, wood accumulates at the site because of the narrow, stable channels created where the river’s flow divides.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Phillips found that the jam is not behind the river’s shift: “Instead, wood accumulates at the site because of the narrow, stable channels created where the river’s flow divides.” The jam is a result of conditions at the site rather than the cause of the shift, so it did not trigger that shift.

A.why_wrong: The text is about what causes what; whether the jam made the shift visible is never discussed.

B.why_wrong: A pile of wood and a change in a river’s course are not compared in the text, so saying the jam did not resemble the shift adds nothing the “Instead” sentence answers.

C.why_wrong: A log-jam cannot measure anything; the text explains that the jam forms because of the channels rather than causing the shift.

items.passage: Household recipe books from early modern England have often been described as the work of women alone. Historian Elaine Leong argues, however, that most were ______ projects. The notebook of medical recipes that Mary Cholmeley brought to Yorkshire when she married Henry Fairfax in 1627, for instance, was supplemented for decades by Mary, Henry, their children, and other relatives.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Leong’s view is set against the idea that the books were “the work of women alone,” and her example shows one notebook “supplemented for decades by Mary, Henry, their children, and other relatives.” Books compiled by many family members working together were collective projects.

A.recipe: reversal: trait of the wrong party (ANT)
A.why_wrong: Solitary work is what the earlier description implies (“the work of women alone”); Leong argues “however” against it, and her example involves a whole family.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns what the books cost; it is about who wrote in them.

D.why_wrong: The notebook was kept and added to by a family for its own use; nothing suggests the books were made for sale.

items.passage: Christopher Achen and Larry Bartels interpreted Woodrow Wilson’s diminished 1916 vote share in New Jersey beach counties after a series of shark attacks as evidence that voters punish incumbents for misfortunes beyond their control. Analyzing presidential elections from 1872 to 2012, however, Anthony Fowler and Andrew B. Hall found no systematic evidence that shark attacks affect elections, suggesting that the 1916 result is ______ voters’ general behavior.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Unrepresentative of means not typical of. Analyzing presidential elections “from 1872 to 2012,” Fowler and Hall “found no systematic evidence that shark attacks affect elections.” If shark attacks do not generally sway elections, then the drop in 1916 that Achen and Bartels cited does not reflect the usual pattern; it is unrepresentative of voters’ general behavior.

A.recipe: reversal: the challenged view’s reading of the result (ANT)
A.why_wrong: Indicative of means serving as a sign of. That is how Achen and Bartels treated the 1916 result, “as evidence that voters punish incumbents for misfortunes beyond their control.” The finding of “no systematic evidence that shark attacks affect elections” across more than a century of elections points the other way.

C.recipe: near miss: right direction, too strong (CONNOT)
C.why_wrong: Antithetical to means directly opposed to. Finding “no systematic evidence that shark attacks affect elections” shows that the 1916 drop is not typical, not that voters generally do the opposite, such as rewarding leaders after shark attacks.

D.why_wrong: Ancillary to means supplementary or subordinate to. The text compares the 1916 result with the general pattern in elections; it does not present the result as a secondary part of voters’ behavior.

sources.what: Fowler and Hall 2018, Journal of Politics 80(4), abstract: data on every fatal shark attack in US history and county returns from every presidential election 1872 to 2012 show no systematic evidence that shark attacks affect elections; Achen and Bartels’s New Jersey 1916 finding weakens under alternative specifications

items.passage: Store-brand and national-brand headache remedies are physically interchangeable products, yet Bart Bronnenberg and colleagues found that while the average shopper chooses the national brand 26 percent of the time, pharmacists do so only 9 percent of the time. The researchers concluded that the extra price such brands command for health products is, to a sizable degree, ______ shoppers’ misinformation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A function of something is a quantity that depends on it. The remedies “are physically interchangeable products,” yet pharmacists, who know this, choose the national brand “only 9 percent of the time,” compared with “26 percent” for the average shopper. Since the better informed pay the extra price less often, the size of that price depends on how misinformed shoppers are: it is a function of their misinformation.

A.why_wrong: A casualty of something is harmed or destroyed by it. The text suggests the opposite: misinformation sustains the extra price, since the best-informed shoppers, pharmacists, are the ones who rarely pay it.

B.recipe: near miss: right relation, reversed order (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: A precursor to something comes before it and leads to it. That would make the extra price a cause of shoppers’ misinformation, but the comparison with pharmacists suggests that misinformation is what produces the extra price.

C.why_wrong: A palliative for something eases its effects. Nothing in the text suggests that paying more for a national brand relieves shoppers’ misinformation; the shoppers who pay it are simply less informed.

sources.what: Bronnenberg, Dube, Gentzkow, Shapiro, Do Pharmacists Buy Bayer? (NBER w20295; QJE 2015), abstract: physically homogeneous categories; pharmacists choose national-brand headache remedies only 9 percent of the time against 26 percent for the average consumer; misinformation explains a sizable share of the brand premium for health products

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Key letter D. Band-7 moves: a familiar word in a transferred, mathematical sense (a function of); three steps (the products are the same, the informed rarely pay extra, so the premium tracks misinformation); near miss a precursor to fails only on direction. attributable to is already a WiC key (w2b2_02), so not used. Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): a casualty of 46,751; a precursor to 38,574; a palliative for 39,851; a function of 8,622. Key not the longest option.

items.passage: Superionic water ice, whose structure physicist Marius Millot and colleagues confirmed in 2019 using laser-driven shock compression and X-ray diffraction, is a ______ substance: its oxygen atoms remain fixed in a crystalline lattice, as in any solid, while its hydrogen ions diffuse through that lattice as readily as they would through a liquid.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Paradoxical means seeming to combine features that contradict each other. The text explains that superionic ice’s “oxygen atoms remain fixed in a crystalline lattice, as in any solid, while its hydrogen ions diffuse through that lattice as readily as they would through a liquid.” A substance that behaves like a solid and a liquid at once is paradoxical.

B.recipe: near miss: fits the liquid half of the clue only (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: Volatile means likely to evaporate or change suddenly. The hydrogen ions move freely, but the text says nothing about the ice evaporating or being unstable, and its oxygen atoms “remain fixed in a crystalline lattice.”

C.recipe: topic echo: a property of solids (ASSOC)
C.why_wrong: Brittle describes a solid that breaks easily. The text never discusses how the ice breaks; its point is that the substance is solid in one respect and liquid-like in another.

D.why_wrong: Inert means inactive or motionless. The text says the hydrogen ions “diffuse through that lattice,” so part of the substance is in constant motion.

sources.what: Millot et al. 2019, Nature 569: 251-255, abstract: superionic water ice has liquid-like protons diffusing through the solid lattice of oxygen; laser-driven shock waves and X-ray diffraction gave unambiguous evidence of its crystalline oxygen lattice

items.notes: Subject: natural science (physics). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (see the solid trait and the liquid trait, then name what their combination is). Band 6 by plan: a plain hard key with the clue after a colon, as in 3.4 (variable); volatile is true of the liquid-like half only. Protons simplified to hydrogen ions. Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): paradoxical 28,519; volatile 18,078; brittle 22,307; inert 12,899. Key is the longest option.

items.passage: Sweet taste is often assumed to be ______ to sugar’s appeal. But in a 2008 study, neuroscientist Ivan de Araujo and colleagues found that mice genetically altered so that they could not taste sweetness still developed a strong preference for sugar water over plain water, apparently guided only by the calories that the sugar supplied.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Intrinsic to means essential to, part of the very nature of. The word “But” signals that the finding challenges the assumption. Mice that “could not taste sweetness still developed a strong preference for sugar water over plain water,” so sugar’s appeal did not depend on its taste. The assumption being challenged, then, is that sweet taste is intrinsic to sugar’s appeal.

A.recipe: near miss: right field, too weak (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: Germane means relevant. The finding does not show that taste plays no part in sugar’s appeal for animals that can taste it; it shows that the appeal survives without taste, which challenges the idea that taste is essential, not the idea that it is relevant.

B.recipe: reversal: the finding’s own conclusion offered as the old view (ANT)
B.why_wrong: Incidental means minor or not essential. That is what the finding suggests about sweet taste, so if it had been the usual assumption, “But” would introduce no challenge.

D.why_wrong: Deleterious means harmful. If sweet taste had been assumed to harm sugar’s appeal, a finding that mice preferred sugar without tasting its sweetness would not contrast with that view, as “But” requires.

sources.what: de Araujo et al. 2008, Neuron 57(6): 930-941, Food reward in the absence of taste receptor signaling, abstract: food palatability plays central roles in intake; trpm5-/- mice, which lack the cellular machinery required for sweet taste transduction, can develop a robust preference for sucrose solutions based solely on caloric content

items.passage:
The following text is from Jane Austen’s 1817 novel Persuasion. More than seven years earlier, Anne Elliot, who lives at her family’s estate of Kellynch, ended her engagement to Frederick Wentworth, a young naval officer.

No one had ever come within the Kellynch circle, who could bear a comparison with Frederick Wentworth, as he stood in her memory. No second attachment, the only thoroughly natural, happy, and sufficient cure, at her time of life, had been possible to the <u>nice</u> tone of her mind, the fastidiousness of her taste, in the small limits of the society around them.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “nice” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used in the text, “nice” most nearly means exacting, or hard to satisfy. The sentence explains why no “second attachment” had been possible for Anne: “No one had ever come within the Kellynch circle, who could bear a comparison with Frederick Wentworth,” and the nice tone of her mind is paired with “the fastidiousness of her taste.” A mind that turns away everyone who falls short of so high a standard is exacting.

A.why_wrong: Nice often means agreeable, but an agreeable tone of mind would not explain why no “second attachment” had been possible. The text pairs the nice tone of Anne’s mind with “the fastidiousness of her taste”: it is what keeps her from accepting anyone, not what makes her pleasant.

B.why_wrong: Tone can describe sound, but here it describes the character of Anne’s mind. Nothing in the text concerns music or her voice.

D.recipe: another sense of the target, near the everyday one (SENSE)
D.why_wrong: A nice person may be kind, but kindness is not what has prevented a second attachment. The text explains that no one “could bear a comparison with Frederick Wentworth” and links the nice tone of her mind to “the fastidiousness of her taste,” so the word describes how demanding she is.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg, Jane Austen, Persuasion (1817), chapter IV (text copied exactly)

items.passage: Bahamian artist Tavares Strachan’s practice is thoroughly ______: his projects have included undergoing cosmonaut training in Russia, launching a small satellite into space in collaboration with a museum’s technology laboratory, and transporting a 2.5-ton block of ice from the Alaskan Arctic to the Bahamas for display in a solar-powered freezer at his former elementary school.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Interdisciplinary means combining or crossing several fields of knowledge. Each example joins art to another field: his projects have included “undergoing cosmonaut training in Russia,” “launching a small satellite into space in collaboration with a museum’s technology laboratory,” and displaying a block of Arctic ice “in a solar-powered freezer.” A practice that keeps bringing together art, space science, and engineering is interdisciplinary.

B.why_wrong: Parochial means narrow or limited to local concerns. The examples reach from Russia to orbit to the Arctic, so the practice is anything but narrow.

C.why_wrong: Derivative means imitative of others’ work. Nothing in the text suggests that Strachan copies other artists; the examples are unusual projects of his own.

D.recipe: near miss: half fits the space projects (CONNOT)
D.why_wrong: Speculative means based on conjecture rather than fact. Space travel may sound speculative, but the examples are things Strachan actually did, such as “undergoing cosmonaut training” and “launching a small satellite.”

sources.what: Wikipedia, Tavares Strachan: practice examines the intersection of art, science and the environment; cosmonaut training at the Yuri Gagarin Training Center (Orthostatic Tolerance); ENOCH satellite launched 2018 with the LACMA Art + Technology Lab; 2.5-ton block of Alaskan Arctic ice shipped to the Bahamas and displayed in a solar-powered freezer (2006)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (visual art). Key letter A. Band 6 by plan (B4 hard): the abstract category the three examples share, as undifferentiated in 3.18; distractors are other categories the examples half fit (speculative for the space projects, parochial for a Bahamian focus). Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): interdisciplinary 32,400; parochial 22,657; derivative 31,569; speculative 12,208. Key is the longest option.

band7.why: planned band 6 (band_target 6); the key is the plain category the three examples point at, and the near miss speculative is answered by the examples being things he did, so a strong band 6

items.passage: Analyzing data from Massachusetts, economist Joshua Goodman found that school closures during heavy snowstorms did not measurably reduce achievement, whereas individual absences caused by moderate snowfall did. A closure, which affects an entire class simultaneously, is apparently less ______ than an absence, since teachers can more readily accommodate an interruption that every student experiences together.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Disruptive means interfering with normal progress. Goodman found that closures “did not measurably reduce achievement,” whereas absences did, and the text explains that “teachers can more readily accommodate an interruption that every student experiences together.” A closure, then, is less disruptive to learning than an absence.

A.recipe: near miss: describes length, not effect (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: Prolonged means long-lasting. The text compares how much closures and absences hurt achievement, not how long they last.

B.why_wrong: Conspicuous means easily noticed. Nothing in the text concerns how noticeable closures are, and a closure for the whole school would hardly be less noticeable than one student’s absence.

C.why_wrong: Advantageous means helpful. Saying a closure is less advantageous than an absence would make absences the better outcome, the opposite of what Goodman found.

sources.what: Goodman 2014, Flaking Out: Student Absences and Snow Days as Disruptions of Instructional Time (NBER w20221), abstract: strong relationship between student absences and achievement but no impact of lost instructional time due to school closures, Massachusetts; teachers deal well with coordinated disruptions like snow days but poorly with absences that affect different students at different times

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics of education). Key letter D. Negation sits in a comparative (less ______ than), as in medium B5 items; the clue is the since clause plus the first sentence’s finding. Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): prolonged 5,313; conspicuous 6,466; advantageous 17,474; disruptive absent. Key not the longest option.

items.passage: Artist Kapwani Kiwanga’s ongoing project Flowers for Africa begins with archival photographs of the bouquets and garlands displayed at ceremonies commemorating African nations’ independence. Rather than copying an arrangement exactly, each florist who collaborates with Kiwanga re-creates it in their own style, so the bouquets that viewers encounter are best understood as ______ the archival images.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Interpretations of something are versions that express someone’s own understanding of it. The text says that “Rather than copying an arrangement exactly, each florist who collaborates with Kiwanga re-creates it in their own style.” Bouquets made this way are interpretations of the archival images.

A.why_wrong: Replicas are exact copies. The text says the florists re-create each arrangement “Rather than copying an arrangement exactly,” so the bouquets are not replicas.

C.why_wrong: A rebuttal argues against something. Nothing suggests that the bouquets dispute the photographs; they are based on them.

D.why_wrong: Precursors come before the thing they lead to. The bouquets are made from photographs taken long ago, so they come after the images, not before.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Kapwani Kiwanga: Flowers for Africa (2013 to ongoing) uses archival images of independence ceremonies; bouquets, garlands and centerpieces captured on film are shown to florists, who appropriate them in their own compositional language; the reconstructed arrangements are displayed and left to wilt

Clue is a restatement in the same sentence (rather than copying ... in their own style); one near miss (replicas of), one order reversal, one unsupported. items.passage: Antibiotic resistance in disease-causing bacteria is often regarded as a by-product of modern medicine. But Jesper Larsen and colleagues showed that methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus ______ the clinical use of antibiotics: one resistant lineage emerged in European hedgehogs, whose skin can host a fungus that produces penicillin-like antibiotics, before such drugs entered medicine.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Predates means came earlier than. The text explains that “one resistant lineage emerged in European hedgehogs ... before such drugs entered medicine.” Resistance that arose before doctors began using antibiotics predates the clinical use of antibiotics.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that resistance in these bacteria sped up the medical use of antibiotics; the text is concerned with when the resistance first appeared.

C.why_wrong: If resistance followed the clinical use of antibiotics, it would have appeared afterward, which is the view the text rejects: the lineage emerged “before such drugs entered medicine.”

D.recipe: near miss: a parallel, wrong timing (CONNOT)
D.why_wrong: Mirrors would mean that resistance rose and spread along with medical use of antibiotics. The text says instead that it emerged in hedgehogs before that use began, driven by a fungus on their skin.

items.explanation: Vestigial describes a part or system that remains after it has lost most or all of its original function. Humans “do not orient their ears toward sounds,” yet in the muscles around the ear “activity increased on the side of whichever sound a listener was attending to,” and the system that “once directed our ancestors’ ears” is described as a “neural fossil” that has persisted “for about 25 million years.” A system that still stirs but no longer turns the ears is vestigial.

A.recipe: near miss: inactive rather than reduced (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: Dormant means inactive for the time being but able to become active again. The text shows the system is not inactive: in the muscles around the ear, “activity increased on the side of whichever sound a listener was attending to.” Nor does anything suggest the system will one day turn people’s ears again; it is a leftover, a “neural fossil.”

C.why_wrong: Nascent means just beginning to develop. The text calls the system a “neural fossil” that “once directed our ancestors’ ears” and has persisted “for about 25 million years,” so it is old and reduced, not newly emerging.

D.why_wrong: Compensatory means making up for a loss. The text does not say the muscles’ activity makes up for anything, such as the inability to point the ears; it presents the activity as a remnant of an old system.

sources.what: Strauss et al. 2020, eLife 9:e54536, PubMed abstract: unlike dogs and cats, people do not point their ears; humans may have retained a vestigial pinna-orienting system that has persisted as a neural fossil for about 25 million years; ear-muscle EMG activity was larger at the ear on the side of the attended stimulus

items.notes: Subject: natural science (human biology, neuroscience). Key letter B. Replaces the withdrawn Megaponera claim (concept duplicate of official TSP item 3e63fce0). Band-7 moves (spec/rw/band7/words_in_context.md section 5, B1): a rare key the clue restates only figuratively (“neural fossil”, “once directed our ancestors’ ears”), as plethora restates ubiquity in bce4d106; a near-synonym distractor failing on one feature (dormant: inactive and able to revive, but the muscles are active); reversal nascent; unsupported compensatory.
