items.passage:
The following text is from Joseph Conrad’s 1917 novella The Shadow-Line. The narrator, a young captain whose crew has been weakened by fever, goes down to the deck of his ship on a dark night.

I descended the ladder to the quarter-deck. The starlight seemed to die out before reaching that spot, but when I asked quietly: “Are you there, men?” my eyes <u>made out</u> shadow forms starting up around me, very few, very indistinct; and a voice spoke: “All here, sir.”
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “made out” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used in the text, “made out” most nearly means managed to see. The narrator says, “The starlight seemed to die out before reaching that spot,” yet his eyes made out “shadow forms starting up around me, very few, very indistinct.” In near darkness, he was just able to see the men.

A.why_wrong: To make out can mean to fill out, as in making out a check, but the narrator is not writing anything; his “eyes” are picking out “shadow forms.”

B.recipe: another sense of the target, near the key (SENSE)
B.why_wrong: To make out can mean to understand, as in making out what someone means, but here the narrator’s “eyes” are doing the work: in the dark, he barely sees “shadow forms starting up around me.”

D.why_wrong: To make out can mean to get along, as in asking how someone made out, but the narrator is describing what he could see “very indistinct” in the dark, not how he got along with the men.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg #451, Joseph Conrad, The Shadow-Line: A Confession (1917), chapter V, the narrator goes down to the quarter-deck at night (text copied exactly)

items.notes: Subject: literature (novella, 1917). Key letter C. Phrasal target with phrase options, as in official 1.30 (reaching: Arriving at, Consulting with, Running to, Clinging to); every distractor is another sense of make out, one of them (understand) close to the key but ruled out because the eyes do the work. Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): Filled out 727; Came to understand 328; Managed to see 1,880; Got along with 338. Key is not the longest option.

items.passage: Conventional economic models presume that consumers’ willingness to pay for a product is ______ the payment method they use. Yet marketing researchers Drazen Prelec and Duncan Simester found that participants’ valuations of sporting-event tickets increased by as much as 100 percent when they were instructed to use a credit card rather than cash.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Unrelated to means having no connection with. “Yet” signals that Prelec and Simester’s finding runs against the conventional models. The finding is that participants’ valuations of the same tickets “increased by as much as 100 percent when they were instructed to use a credit card rather than cash,” so the payment method does change what people will pay. The models that this finding contradicts must therefore presume that willingness to pay is unrelated to the payment method.

A.recipe: reversal: the finding’s own conclusion, placed in the view it contradicts (ANT)
A.why_wrong: Contingent on means depending on. That is what Prelec and Simester’s result shows, since valuations “increased by as much as 100 percent” with a credit card. But “Yet” presents the result as a challenge to the conventional models, so the models cannot already hold that the amount depends on the payment method.

C.why_wrong: Subordinate to means ranked below or less important than. The text never ranks willingness to pay against the payment method; it asks only whether the method affects what people will pay.

D.recipe: near miss: a dependence of degree, the wrong relation (CONNOT)
D.why_wrong: Proportional to means rising and falling in step with. That would still make willingness to pay depend on the payment method, which is what the finding introduced by “Yet” shows, not what the conventional models presume; a method of payment is also not a quantity that a valuation could rise in step with.

sources.what: Prelec and Simester 2001, Marketing Letters 12(1), abstract (publisher page): in genuine transactions of potentially high value, willingness to pay can be increased when customers are instructed to use a credit card rather than cash; the effect may be large (up to 100%)
MIT News clip of Bloomberg coverage: in Prelec and Simester's study credit card buyers were willing to pay over 100% more for tickets; Wikipedia on Prelec: tickets to sporting events

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics). Key letter B. Band 6 by plan. Steps: 2 (the finding shows payment method matters; “Yet” puts the blank on the view the finding contradicts, so the key is the opposite of the finding). Received view then finding, with the blank in the received view, as in 3.10 and 3.12. Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): contingent on 17,762; unrelated to 40,068; subordinate to 13,590; proportional to 68,085. independent of is official 3.2’s key, so not used. Key not the longest option.

review.note: Batch note checked: Springer abstract says willingness to pay can be increased with a credit card, effect up to 100%; passage says as much as 100 percent, no stronger. Sporting-event tickets confirmed on Wikipedia (Drazen Prelec); MIT clip of Bloomberg says over 100% more for tickets.

band7.why: Planned band 6 and it meets it. Received view then finding with the blank on the view the finding overturns, as in 3.10 and 3.12; the reversal contingent on is the finding’s own conclusion and proportional to is a near miss that still makes the amount depend on the method; all four options past rank 10,000 (raw contingent 17,762, unrelated 40,068, subordinate 13,590, proportional 68,085); two steps.

items.passage: Many African American artists of the 1970s made expressive, overtly political art, but conceptual artist Charles Gaines ______ that approach: in series such as Walnut Tree Orchard, begun in 1975, he plotted photographs of trees onto numbered grids according to a fixed system, producing abstract, rule-governed works rather than direct statements about race or politics.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Eschewed means deliberately avoided. The word “but” sets Gaines apart from the artists who “made expressive, overtly political art,” and the clause after the colon says what he made instead: photographs of trees plotted “onto numbered grids according to a fixed system,” “abstract, rule-governed works rather than direct statements about race or politics.” He kept away from the expressive, political approach; the text does not say he copied it or attacked it.

B.why_wrong: Emulated means imitated in an effort to match. The word “but” and “rather than direct statements about race or politics” show that Gaines did not follow the approach of the artists who made “overtly political art.”

C.recipe: near miss: right direction, wrong act (CONNOT)
C.why_wrong: Disparaged means spoke of as having little worth. The text describes only what Gaines made instead, “abstract, rule-governed works”; it never says he criticized other artists or their approach.

D.why_wrong: Parodied means imitated in order to mock. Gaines’s grids of trees do not imitate political art at all; they are “abstract, rule-governed works rather than direct statements about race or politics.”

sources.what: Wikipedia, Charles Gaines (artist): work involves systems, predominantly the grid, often with photography; in the 1970s, when political expressionism was a prevailing concern among African-American artists, Gaines was an outlier in his pursuit of abstraction and non-didactic approach to race and politics; with Walnut Tree Orchard (1975-2014) he began working with photographs, continuing the use of grid paper

items.notes: Subject: humanities (visual art). Key letter A. Band-7 moves: rare key with all four options past rank 20,000 (raw freq.txt: eschewed 36,027; emulated 26,669; disparaged 36,547; parodied 47,407); the clue after the colon restates the key in a different register (an approach he set aside by making something else), as “this rejection is evident” does for repudiates in 93665100; near miss disparaged fails on one feature (avoiding is not criticizing), like recants against repudiates. Steps: 2 (contrast with the 1970s norm, then the alternative he chose). Numbered grids per the Hauser and Wirth and meer.com descriptions of his tree series. Key not the longest option.

review.note: Core claim (1970s, outlier pursuing abstraction and systems against prevailing political expressionism; Walnut Tree Orchard 1975-2014, photographs with grids) checked on Wikipedia.

band7.why: Vocabulary-carried B1 as in 93665100 (repudiates): all four options past rank 20,000 (raw eschewed 36,027, emulated 26,669, disparaged 36,547, parodied 47,407), key past 20,000 so the combined gate passes; near miss disparaged fails on one feature (avoiding is not criticizing), like recants against repudiates; two steps (the contrast with the 1970s norm, then the alternative he chose). Rarest distractor just under 50,000, so check 2 alone misses.

items.passage: In the Ebbinghaus illusion, a circle surrounded by large circles looks smaller than an identical circle surrounded by small ones. Testing the illusion among the Himba people of northern Namibia, Jan de Fockert and colleagues found that it still occurred but was weaker than among English participants, so the Himba judged the circles’ sizes more accurately—a result that undercuts assumptions of the illusion’s ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Invariance means the quality of staying the same in every case. The illusion “still occurred but was weaker” among the Himba “than among English participants,” so its strength differs from one group of people to another. A result showing that the illusion is not equally strong everywhere undercuts assumptions of its invariance.

A.why_wrong: Plasticity means the capacity to change or be shaped. An illusion that is “weaker” in one group than in another appears to vary with people’s backgrounds, so the result supports, rather than undercuts, the idea of its plasticity.

B.recipe: near miss: right field, fails on one feature (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: Ubiquity means being found everywhere. The text says the illusion “still occurred” among the Himba, so the result does not cast doubt on its presence across groups, only on its having the same strength in all of them.

C.why_wrong: Antiquity means great age. The study compares how strongly two groups experience the illusion today; it says nothing about how old the illusion is.

sources.what: de Fockert, Davidoff, Fagot, Parron, Goldstein 2007, J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 33(3):738-742, abstract: the Ebbinghaus illusion was experienced less strongly by Himba compared with English participants, leading to more accurate size contrast judgments

items.notes: Subject: social science (cross-cultural psychology). Key letter D. Band-7 moves: the negation is hidden in a verb (undercuts assumptions of, as preclude claims of in 6017ae31); all four options past rank 10,000 and three past 50,000 (raw freq.txt: plasticity 67,984; ubiquity and invariance absent; antiquity 11,853); near miss ubiquity fails on one feature (presence everywhere against sameness everywhere), and the passage says the illusion “still occurred” so that ubiquity is cleanly wrong; reversal plasticity is the trait the finding supports. Steps: 3 (weaker in one group, so its strength varies, so an assumption of sameness is undercut). Key ties plasticity as the longest option (10 letters).

review.note: Core claim checked on the PubMed abstract (illusion experienced less strongly by Himba than English participants, more accurate size judgments).

band7.why: Negation hidden in a verb (undercuts assumptions of), as preclude in 6017ae31; all four options past rank 10,000 with ubiquity and invariance unseen; near miss ubiquity fails on one feature (presence everywhere against sameness everywhere) and is closed by still occurred; reversal plasticity is the trait the finding supports; three linked steps.

items.passage: Though the giant panda is a large carnivoran whose digestive tract is poorly adapted to its specialized bamboo diet, Yonggang Nie and colleagues concluded that the animal subsists on that diet partly because its metabolism is surprisingly ______. Undersized vital organs, minimal physical activity, and depressed levels of thyroid hormones keep the panda’s daily energy expenditure considerably below that of most mammals of comparable size.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Sluggish means slow or inactive. “Though” sets the panda’s size and its “digestive tract is poorly adapted to its specialized bamboo diet” against its survival on that diet, and “surprisingly” marks the reason as unexpected for “a large carnivoran.” The second sentence explains it: organs, activity, and hormones “keep the panda’s daily energy expenditure considerably below that of most mammals of comparable size.” A metabolism that uses so little energy is sluggish.

A.recipe: reversal: the expectation the contrast overturns (ANT)
A.why_wrong: Brisk means quick and energetic. That is what one might expect of “a large carnivoran,” but “surprisingly” signals the opposite, and the text says the panda’s energy expenditure is “considerably below that of most mammals of comparable size.”

B.recipe: near miss: a slow metabolism of the wrong kind (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: Seasonal means changing with the seasons. A hibernating animal’s metabolism slows in winter, but the text describes a panda whose energy expenditure stays low because of its “vital organs,” “minimal physical activity,” and “depressed levels of thyroid hormones,” with no mention of seasons.

D.why_wrong: Volatile means liable to change suddenly. The text describes a metabolism that is consistently low, not one that swings unpredictably.

sources.what: Nie, Speakman et al. 2015, Science 349:171-174, abstract: the carnivoran giant panda has a specialized bamboo diet to which its alimentary tract is poorly adapted; daily energy expenditure of five captive and three wild pandas averaged 37.7% of the predicted value; achieved in part by reduced sizes of several vital organs and low physical activity; thyroid hormone levels well below those expected for a mammal of comparable size

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal physiology). Key letter C. Band 6 by plan. Steps: 2 (a large carnivoran on a poor diet would be expected to burn energy fast; Though and surprisingly reverse that expectation, and the second sentence confirms the low expenditure). Concessive frame as in 3.7 and 3.20. Replaces a mantis shrimp colour-vision draft (a live Boundaries item and a round-1 subject). Raw freq.txt ranks: brisk 5,598; seasonal 45,224; sluggish 11,947; volatile 18,078. Key ties seasonal and volatile as the longest option.

fixes: determined changed to concluded: the Science abstract says the low expenditure likely enables pandas to survive on bamboo, so the passage no longer states the finding more strongly than the source
review.note: Core claim checked on the PubMed abstract (daily energy expenditure 37.7% of predicted; reduced organ sizes, low activity, low thyroid hormones).

band7.why: Planned band 6. Concessive frame (Though ... surprisingly) with the clue in the next sentence; three of four options past rank 10,000 (raw sluggish 11,947, seasonal 45,224, volatile 18,078; brisk 5,598); reversal brisk is the expectation for a large carnivoran, near miss seasonal a slow metabolism of the wrong kind. A plain key restated by the second sentence keeps it at 6.

items.passage:
The following text is from Henry James’s 1897 novel The Spoils of Poynton. Fleda Vetch is staying with her friend Mrs. Gereth at Ricks, Mrs. Gereth’s house in the country.

Fleda was not only a brilliant creature, but she heard herself commended in these days for new and strange attractions; she <u>figured</u> suddenly, in the queer conversations of Ricks, as a distinguished, almost as a dangerous beauty. That retouching of her hair and dress in which her friend had impulsively indulged on a first glimpse of her secret was by implication very frequently repeated.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “figured” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used in the text, “figured” means appeared or was presented. Fleda “heard herself commended” for “new and strange attractions,” and in the “conversations of Ricks” she was presented “as a distinguished, almost as a dangerous beauty” while her friend kept retouching “her hair and dress.” She appeared in that role in other people’s talk.

A.why_wrong: To figure can mean to calculate, as in figuring a sum, but nothing in the text involves working out numbers; the sentence is about how Fleda was spoken of.

C.why_wrong: To figure can mean to picture in the mind, but the text says Fleda “heard herself commended”: the image of her as a beauty came from the “conversations of Ricks” and her friend’s retouching of “her hair and dress,” not from Fleda imagining herself that way.

D.why_wrong: To figure can mean to conclude or decide, but Fleda makes no decision in the text; the sentence describes how she was portrayed in the talk at Ricks.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #33325, Henry James, The Spoils of Poynton (1897); excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel). Key letter B. Band 6 by plan. All three distractors are other senses of figure (calculate, picture, conclude), as in 3.11, where every distractor is a sense of determine; Imagined fits the grammar loosely and is ruled out by “heard herself commended” and the friend’s retouching. Dense, late-James syntax carries part of the difficulty. Raw freq.txt ranks: Calculated 5,304; Appeared 544; Imagined 1,283; Decided 1,114. Target figured. The Spoils of Poynton is not used in any official item (grep of all transcripts and cb_api). Excerpt 62 words. Key not the longest option.

review.note: Excerpt copied exactly from Gutenberg 33325; Fleda at Ricks with Mrs. Gereth confirmed from context.

band7.why: Planned band 6. Common target in a secondary sense with three real senses of figure as distractors, as in 9b22bf7b (determine/Dictate); the key Appeared is rank 544, so the band rests on the late-James syntax and the loose fit of Imagined, acceptable for a planned 6, not a band-7 M1 (no mid-frequency key).

items.passage: Lake Vida, in Antarctica, is capped by permanent ice, and the extremely salty brine sealed beneath it is about −13°C, contains no dissolved oxygen, and has been cut off from external sources of energy for millennia. Nevertheless, Alison Murray and colleagues determined that this inhospitable brine is far from ______: it harbors a phylogenetically diverse, metabolically active bacterial community.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Sterile means free of living things. Despite the brine’s harsh conditions, Murray and colleagues determined that “it harbors a phylogenetically diverse, metabolically active bacterial community,” so the brine is far from sterile.

B.why_wrong: The text says the brine “has been cut off from external sources of energy for millennia,” so it is isolated; saying it is far from isolated contradicts the text.

C.why_wrong: Saline means salty, and the text calls the water “extremely salty brine,” so it is not far from saline.

D.why_wrong: Transparent means clear enough to see through. The text says nothing about how clear the brine is; the colon introduces a point about the life it holds.

sources.what: Murray et al. 2012, PNAS 109(50):20626-31, abstract: the permanent ice cover of Lake Vida encapsulates a cryogenic brine (-13 C, salinity 200), aphotic and anoxic; a phylogenetically diverse and metabolically active Bacteria-dominated assemblage was observed in the brine; unusual given the millennial scale of its isolation from external sources of energy

items.notes: Subject: natural science (microbiology). Key letter A. Negated frame (far from) with a Nevertheless concession; two negation-flip distractors and one unsupported word, the band-5 B5 mix. Brine temperature given as the abstract’s -13 C. Raw freq.txt ranks: sterile 24,607; isolated 7,655; saline 32,943; transparent 7,165. lifeless is an earlier WiC key, so not used. Key not the longest option.

review.note: Core claim checked on the PubMed abstract (-13 C anoxic brine, diverse metabolically active bacteria, millennial isolation from external energy).

items.passage: At Hudson’s Bay Company trading posts, all merchandise was priced in “made beaver,” a unit equivalent to one prime beaver pelt in good condition, and the company subsequently issued brass tokens denominated in made beaver and fractions thereof. Consequently, the made beaver functioned not merely as a tradable commodity but also as ______ value.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A yardstick for something is a standard for measuring it. Because “all merchandise was priced in ‘made beaver,’” and the company even “issued brass tokens denominated in made beaver and fractions thereof,” the unit was used to state what everything was worth. It functioned as a yardstick for value as well as “a tradable commodity.”

A.recipe: near miss: right field, wrong relation (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: A guarantee of something makes it certain. The brass tokens might suggest that the unit backed something’s worth, but the text says only that merchandise “was priced in” made beaver, which makes the unit a measure of value; it never says the unit assured that merchandise was worth anything.

B.why_wrong: A hindrance to something gets in its way. Nothing in the text suggests the made beaver interfered with value; it was the unit in which value was expressed.

D.why_wrong: An outgrowth of something is a development that grows out of it. The text presents the made beaver as the unit used to set prices, not as something that developed out of value.

sources.what: The Canadian Encyclopedia, Made Beaver: a Standard of Trade was established based on the made beaver (one prime beaver skin in good condition); prices of all goods were set in Made Beaver; later the HBC issued brass tokens in denominations of one Made Beaver and fractions thereof

items.notes: Subject: history (economic history). Key letter C. Restatement through consequence: prices set in the unit, tokens issued in it, so it measured value. Near miss a guarantee of plays on the tokens. Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): guarantee 10,832; hindrance 14,036; yardstick 74,915; outgrowth 46,141. a gauge of, a barometer of and a proxy for are earlier WiC keys, so not used. Key ties an outgrowth of as the longest option.

review.note: Core claim checked on The Canadian Encyclopedia via WebFetch (curl blocked): standard of trade on the made beaver, all prices set in it, later brass tokens of one made beaver and fractions.

items.passage: South African artist Igshaan Adams bases numerous tapestries on desire lines, the informal footpaths that emerge when pedestrians repeatedly ______ a designated paved route in favor of a shared shortcut, trampling vegetation until a new trail becomes visible. Incorporating rope, wire, shells, and beads, his woven works chart such pathways in Bonteheuwel, a segregated working-class township of Cape Town where he grew up.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To bypass something is to go around it instead of using it. Desire lines emerge when pedestrians leave “a designated paved route in favor of a shared shortcut,” trampling vegetation “until a new trail becomes visible,” so they bypass the paved route.

A.why_wrong: To retrace a route is to follow it again. The pedestrians who make desire lines take “a shared shortcut” instead of the paved route, so they do not follow it.

B.why_wrong: To obstruct a route is to block it. The text says pedestrians choose a shortcut over the paved route, not that they keep others from using it.

C.recipe: topic echo: what planners do with routes (ASSOC)
C.why_wrong: To survey a route is to examine or measure it. Pedestrians who take “a shared shortcut” are simply crossing the ground, not measuring the paved route.

items.passage: Charon, Pluto’s largest satellite, displays a distinctive dark red cap at its northern pole. Planetary scientist Will Grundy and colleagues modeled its formation: because Charon’s poles become extraordinarily cold during their prolonged winters, they can ______ gas escaping from Pluto’s atmosphere, retaining it on the surface while ultraviolet radiation converts it into complex, reddish organic molecules.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To trap something is to catch and hold it. Because Charon’s poles “become extraordinarily cold,” they can catch the gas “escaping from Pluto’s atmosphere,” “retaining it on the surface” while radiation changes it. The poles trap the gas.

A.why_wrong: To repel something is to drive it away. The text says the poles end up “retaining it on the surface,” the opposite of driving the gas away.

C.why_wrong: To dissolve something is to break it down in a liquid. The text describes gas retained on a frozen surface and changed by “ultraviolet radiation,” not gas dissolved in anything.

D.why_wrong: To release something is to let it go. The gas comes from Pluto and is then held at Charon’s poles, so the poles take it in rather than give it off.

sources.what: Grundy et al. 2016, Nature 539:65-68, abstract: Charon’s dark red northern polar cap; gas from Pluto transiently cold-trapped and processed at Charon’s winter pole; model of supply and temporary cold-trapping of material escaping from Pluto and its photolytic processing into more complex, less volatile molecules

items.notes: Subject: natural science (planetary science). Key letter B. Cause clue (because ... extraordinarily cold) and a confirming participle (retaining it on the surface). Photolytic processing given as ultraviolet radiation (the polar night is lit by ultraviolet from the sky, not by sunlight). Raw freq.txt ranks: repel 16,874; trap 3,291; dissolve 18,351; release 3,675. Key shortest option.

review.note: Core claim checked on the PubMed abstract (cold-trapping of gas escaping from Pluto at the winter pole, photolytic processing).

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Leonard Merrick’s 1903 novel The Quaint Companions.

[Mrs. Tremlett] was the widow of a novelist who had written such beautiful prose that many people had been eager to meet him—once. Afterwards they talked less about his prose than his manners. He had left her, their daughter, a policy for five hundred pounds, and an album of carefully pasted Press cuttings. During his life she had suffered with him in furnished apartments; at his death she <u>took to</u> letting them.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “took to” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used in the text, “took to” means began, as a new practice. The text contrasts “During his life,” when Mrs. Tremlett “suffered with him in furnished apartments,” with what she did “at his death”: she began letting, or renting out, such apartments herself.

B.why_wrong: To take to someone or something can mean to grow fond of it, but the text gives no sign that Mrs. Tremlett enjoyed letting apartments; it marks only what she started doing “at his death.”

C.why_wrong: To take to a place can mean to flee there, as in taking to the hills, but nothing in the text involves escape; the phrase introduces what she did for a living after his death.

D.why_wrong: Returned to would mean she had let apartments before. The text says only that she “suffered with him in furnished apartments” during his life; letting them was new “at his death.”

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #43616, Leonard Merrick, The Quaint Companions (1903); excerpt copied exactly except the bracketed name and a closed em dash for the source’s double hyphen

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel). Key letter A. Phrasal target with two real senses as distractors (grow fond of, flee to) and one unsupported reading; letting (renting out) is not needed to answer. Raw freq.txt ranks: Began 241; fond 1,331; Fled 2,251; Returned 365. The Quaint Companions and Merrick are not used in any official item. Excerpt 71 words. Key shortest option.

review.note: Excerpt copied exactly from Gutenberg 43616 except the bracketed name for She and a closed em dash for the double hyphen.

items.passage: Malawian-born artist Billie Zangewa, who lives in Johannesburg, South Africa, creates collages from fragments of raw silk that she cuts and stitches together by hand. Rather than grand public events, her luminous works depict ______ life: scenes from her own household and from her experience of motherhood.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Domestic means relating to the home and family. The text says Zangewa’s works show “scenes from her own household and from her experience of motherhood” rather than “grand public events,” so they depict domestic life.

A.why_wrong: Rural means relating to the countryside. The text says nothing about farms or the country; it describes scenes from Zangewa’s “own household.”

items.passage: Researchers Kyle Barron, Edward Kung, and Davide Proserpio found that the expansion of Airbnb raised residential rents across the United States, apparently because some landlords reallocated housing from long-term leases to short-term rentals. items.passage: Ancient Greek texts typically portray the armies that defended Greek cities as ______, unified by a shared “Greekness.” But when Katherine Reinberger and colleagues analyzed strontium and oxygen isotopes in the tooth enamel of soldiers buried after the 480 BCE Battle of Himera, in Sicily, they found that many originated in regions beyond the island, suggesting that the city’s defenders included foreign mercenaries.

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Male orchid bees gather aromatic compounds from flowers, bark and fungi, store them in pouches on their hind legs and display the resulting perfume at courtship sites. Because the antennae of several species respond strongly to particular compounds that are major ingredients of their own perfume, Lukasz Mitko and colleagues suggest that in those lineages the bees’ sense of smell has become ______ to the substances the species collects.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Attuned to something means adjusted to respond to it. The text says “the antennae of several species respond strongly to particular compounds that are major ingredients of their own perfume,” so in those lineages the bees’ sense of smell has become adjusted to the very substances they collect.

A.why_wrong: Immune to something means unaffected by it. The antennae “respond strongly” to the compounds, the opposite of being unaffected.

B.why_wrong: Averse to something means disliking it. The bees gather these compounds and display them, so nothing suggests they avoid them.

C.recipe: near miss: right relation to the substances, wrong effect (CONNOT)
C.why_wrong: Vulnerable to something means open to harm from it. The text describes a strong response to the compounds, not any harm they do.

sources.what: Mitko et al. 2016, J Exp Biol 219:1467-1475 abstract: male neotropical orchid bees collect odoriferous substances from multiple sources, store them in tibial pouches and expose them at display sites; strong antennal responses for some chemicals present as major compounds in the perfume of the same species suggest sensory specialization within multiple lineages (no close correspondence overall between antennal responses and tibial contents)

items.notes: Subject: natural science (chemical ecology). Key letter D. Reviewer rewrite: the draft said the antennae of each species respond to their own perfume and that the researchers argue perfume and smell are interdependent, stronger than the abstract (some chemicals, multiple lineages, sensory specialization, no close correspondence overall); premise narrowed to the abstract and the key changed from interdependent to attuned (specialized is a live easy key, w3b8_11). The cause sits in a because clause, as in 2.22. Raw freq.txt ranks: immune 30,918; averse 13,878; vulnerable 23,199; attuned 23,893. Key is not the longest option.

fixes: premise overstated the source ('each species', 'argue ... interdependent' against the abstract's 'some chemicals', specialization within multiple lineages and no close correspondence overall): narrowed to the abstract, blank rebuilt as 'has become ______ to' with key attuned and new distractors immune, averse, vulnerable; 'odoriferous' and 'olfactory apparatus' plained

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Thomas Nelson Page’s 1903 novel Gordon Keith. Lois Huntington, employed as a companion in Mrs. Wentworth’s household, has promised Norman that she will remain there.

[Mrs. Wentworth] had little idea how often that quiet girl who took her complaints so calmly was tempted to break her vow of silence, answer her upbraidings, and return home. [I]t was for Norman’s sake that Lois <u>put up with</u> her capriciousness.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “put up with” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The text says that Lois was often “tempted to break her vow of silence, answer her upbraidings, and return home” and that she stayed anyway, for Norman’s sake. To put up with the capriciousness is to bear it without being driven off.

A.why_wrong: Finding fault with the capriciousness would mean complaining about it. The text says Lois kept “her vow of silence” instead of answering her employer.

C.why_wrong: Making excuses for the capriciousness would mean defending it to others. Nothing in the text has Lois explaining Mrs. Wentworth to anyone.

D.why_wrong: To put a stop to something is to end it. The capriciousness continues; what Lois does is stay in spite of it.

sources.what: Public-domain text of Thomas Nelson Page, Gordon Keith (1903), Project Gutenberg eBook 14068; the sentences are copied exactly, with the opening of the third sentence trimmed and marked [I]

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter B. Phrase target with four paraphrase options on one frame, as in 2.8 and 2.26; one distractor is another sense of put up. Excerpt copied exactly; the sentence “And it was on this account and for Norman’s sake that Lois put up with her capriciousness” is trimmed to “[I]t was for Norman’s sake ...” because the preceding sentence it refers to was cut. Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): Found fault with absent; Endured patiently absent; Made excuses for absent; Put a stop to absent. Key is the longest option.

fixes: bare 'She' (Mrs. Wentworth) read as Lois: bracketed '[Mrs. Wentworth]' as CB glosses do; text checked against Gutenberg 14068 (exact apart from the marked trims)

items.passage: Around 724 the Silla monk Hyecho departed Tang China for India and composed an account of the kingdoms he encountered along the route. The surviving copy is ______: the manuscript a French scholar acquired from a cave library in Gansu province in 1908 terminates abruptly at both ends, so his descriptions of the opening and closing stages of the journey are lost.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Incomplete means missing some of its parts. The text says the surviving manuscript “terminates abruptly at both ends, so his descriptions of the opening and closing stages of the journey are lost,” which describes a text that is not all there.

A.why_wrong: Ornate means richly decorated. The text describes what the manuscript is missing, not how it looks.

B.recipe: topic echo: a word for old manuscripts (ASSOC)
B.why_wrong: Handwritten is true of any eighth-century copy and so says nothing about the problem the text raises, which is the missing opening and closing.

C.why_wrong: Disputed would mean that scholars disagree about the copy. The text reports no disagreement; it says part of the account is lost because the manuscript terminates abruptly at both ends.

sources.what: Wang och'onch'ukkuk chon, the travelogue by the Silla monk Hyecho (journey 723 to 727 or 728): the manuscript turned up among the Dunhuang manuscripts and was bought by Paul Pelliot in 1908; it originally had three volumes, of which volume one and the later section of volume three are lost

items.notes: Subject: history. Key letter D. The clue restates the key after the colon, as in official easy B1 items. The cave library is the Mogao complex in Gansu, named only by region so the item does not repeat the Dunhuang star chart subject already claimed in wave 1. Raw freq.txt ranks: ornate 21,070; handwritten absent; disputed 13,888; incomplete 15,991. Key is not the longest option.

fixes: 'the opening and closing stages of his itinerary remain unknown' overstated (the route is known in outline; his account of those stages is lost): now 'his descriptions of ... are lost'; 'composed an account of everything he observed' toned down; source moved to the travelogue page, which states that volume one and the end of volume three are lost; explanation and why_wrong requoted

items.passage: Psychologists Gabriel Radvansky and David Copeland found that walking through a doorway can make a person ______. Participants who carried objects through rooms in a virtual environment had more difficulty remembering the objects after entering a different room than after traveling within the original room.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Forgetful means likely to forget. The text says participants “had more difficulty remembering the objects after entering a different room than after traveling within the original room,” so walking through a doorway made them forget more.

B.why_wrong: Attentive means paying close attention. Participants “had more difficulty remembering the objects” after a change of room, the opposite of sharper attention.

C.why_wrong: Impatient means unwilling to wait. The text measures what people remembered, not how long they were willing to wait.

D.why_wrong: Cautious means careful to avoid danger. Nothing in the text describes participants taking care or avoiding risk; it reports what they remembered.

sources.what: Radvansky and Copeland 2006, Memory & Cognition 34(5):1150-1156 abstract (Walking through doorways causes forgetting): people moving through rooms in a virtual space were probed on objects carried or just set down; information about an object was less available when there was a spatial shift, that is, after going to a new room

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology). Key letter A. Reviewer replacement for a palm-leaf manuscript item: palm leaves as a perishable writing surface are already live in rhetorical_synthesis.GEN.medium.w2b5_18, and it was the third manuscript item in a row here (with Hyecho and book curses) in a humanities-heavy batch. Blank in sentence 1 with the restatement in sentence 2, an official easy B1 pattern (1.10, 1.51). Raw freq.txt ranks: forgetful 10,605; attentive 7,136; impatient 2,549; cautious 5,680. Key ties for the longest option.

fixes: subject replaced (palm leaves as writing surface live in RS w2b5_18; third manuscript item in the batch; humanities-heavy batch): Radvansky and Copeland 2006 doorway forgetting, confirmed from the PubMed abstract; new options checked for a single defensible answer

items.passage: Medieval European scribes sometimes concluded a volume by calling down fever, hanging or excommunication upon anyone who stole it. Inscribed on the final page beside the copyist’s name, such curses operated as a ______ in the centuries before printing, when a stolen manuscript could seldom be replaced.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A deterrent is something that discourages an action. The text says the curses called down punishments “upon anyone who stole it” at a time when “a stolen manuscript could seldom be replaced,” so they were meant to keep thieves off.

A.recipe: topic echo: a word from church practice (ASSOC)
A.why_wrong: A penance is an act performed to show repentance. The curses were aimed at a thief who had not been caught, not at a penitent.

B.why_wrong: A formality is something done merely for form. The text ties the curses to a time “when a stolen manuscript could seldom be replaced,” which gives them a real purpose: keeping the book from being stolen.

C.why_wrong: A tribute is a mark of respect. Threatening a thief with fever and hanging honors nobody.

sources.what: A book curse was a widely used method of discouraging the theft of manuscripts in medieval Europe, generally placed on the first or last page as part of the colophon and invoking excommunication or anathema; an example threatens that the thief “die the death,” suffer “the falling sickness and fever” and be “hanged”

items.notes: Subject: humanities (book history). Key letter D. The clue restates the purpose (the thief, the irreplaceable book). Raw freq.txt ranks: penance 11,096; formality 10,387; tribute 6,590; deterrent 38,922. Key is the longest option.

fixes: why_wrong for formality claimed the text calls the curses 'the real protection a library had', which it does not say: rewritten from the text

items.passage: Hunters in Kachin State, in northern Myanmar, had long recognized a monkey with an upturned face and possessed names for it in two local languages. For zoologists the animal remained ______ until a survey team searching for gibbons obtained a specimen in 2010 and published a formal description the following year.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Unrecorded means not yet set down in the record. The text contrasts hunters who “had long recognized” the monkey with zoologists, who had no description of it until a specimen was obtained in 2010.

B.why_wrong: Commonplace means ordinary and often seen. For zoologists the monkey was not familiar at all; they had no account of it before 2010.

C.recipe: near miss: right field, wrong claim (CONNOT)
C.why_wrong: Legendary would mean known only through stories. The hunters’ knowledge was firsthand, and the text says only that zoologists lacked a description.

D.why_wrong: Abundant means present in large numbers. The text says nothing about how many of these monkeys there are.

sources.what: The Myanmar snub-nosed monkey (Rhinopithecus strykeri) was first found in 2010 in northeastern Kachin State by a team researching the hoolock gibbon, led by Thomas Geissmann and Ngwe Lwin, and formally described in the American Journal of Primatology in 2011; Lisu and Law Waw names for it mean “monkey with an upturned face”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (zoology). Key letter A. Restatement clue across the contrast between hunters and zoologists. Raw freq.txt ranks: unrecorded 38,093; commonplace 3,925; legendary 18,275; abundant 6,940. Key is not the longest option.

items.passage: Wilson Bentley photographed his first snowflake in January 1885 and eventually captured more than five thousand images, catching each crystal on a blackboard and transferring it rapidly onto a microscope slide beneath a bellows camera. Haste was essential, because a snow crystal ______ even at temperatures below freezing: it passes directly into vapor, and a slow photographer is left with nothing to record.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To deteriorate is to break down. The text explains that a crystal “passes directly into vapor” even below freezing, “and a slow photographer is left with nothing to record,” so the crystal is lost while the photographer works.

A.why_wrong: To harden is to become firmer. The text says the crystal passes into vapor even below freezing, which is the opposite of setting hard.

B.why_wrong: To multiply is to increase in number. Nothing in the text suggests a crystal divides; it disappears.

C.recipe: topic echo: a word about photographs (ASSOC)
C.why_wrong: To darken is to grow dim. The photographer is left with nothing because the crystal is gone, not because it loses brightness.

sources.what: Wilson Bentley attached a bellows camera to a compound microscope and photographed his first snowflake on January 15, 1885, capturing more than 5,000 images of crystals; each crystal was caught on a blackboard and transferred rapidly to a microscope slide, and snowflakes are ephemeral even at subzero temperatures because they sublimate

items.notes: Subject: natural science (history of meteorology). Key letter D. The cause sits in a because clause and the colon restates it. Raw freq.txt ranks: hardens 42,898; multiplies 63,727; darkens 28,948; deteriorates 66,161. Key is the longest option.

fixes: unclear last clause ('and the photographic plate preserves nothing') rewritten as 'and a slow photographer is left with nothing to record'; explanation and why_wrong requoted

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Warm water and fresh water are less dense than cold seawater, so a loaded hull settles deeper in them. The depth to which a commercial vessel may legally be loaded is therefore ______: separate markings painted amidships, beside the Plimsoll mark, establish the limit for summer, for winter and for fresh water, and an inspector consults whichever marking applies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Variable means changing with conditions. The text explains that a hull “settles deeper” in warm water and fresh water and that “separate markings painted amidships, beside the Plimsoll mark, establish the limit for summer, for winter and for fresh water,” so the legal depth changes with the water.

B.why_wrong: Uniform means the same in every case. The text says separate markings establish different limits for summer, for winter and for fresh water.

C.why_wrong: Optional means left to choice. The limit is a legal one, and “an inspector consults whichever marking applies,” so it is not up to the ship’s operator.

D.why_wrong: Approximate means roughly correct. Each limit has its own painted marking that an inspector consults, which makes it exact rather than rough.

sources.what: The load line, also known as the Plimsoll line, indicates the legal limit to which a ship may be loaded for specific water types and temperatures; warm water and fresh water are less dense and provide less buoyancy, so the main summer load line is painted amidships with further marks named after the other conditions, such as the winter load line, and the symbol makes it easy for anyone to tell whether a ship is overloaded

items.notes: Subject: natural science and regulation (shipping). Key letter A. Reviewer rewrite: the key graduated was a secondary sense (marked in degrees) of a word students know as finishing school, too hard a move for an easy item, and temporary could be argued for a limit that applies only in summer; the blank now sits on the legal depth and the key is the plain variable. Cause clue in sentence 1 with the examples restating it after the colon. Replaces a Lake Hillier item withdrawn in claims.txt: a pink lake colored by Dunaliella algae is already live as rhetorical_synthesis.EXPL.medium.w2b4_12. Raw freq.txt ranks: variable 20,504 (modern word, about 5,200 corrected); uniform 4,122; optional 60,612 (about 15,600 corrected); approximate 26,836. Key is not the longest option.

fixes: easy key graduated (a secondary sense) replaced: blank moved to the legal depth, key variable, distractor temporary (arguable for a summer-only limit) replaced by optional; explanation and why_wrong rewritten

items.passage: The painters of the Worpswede colony, where Paula Modersohn-Becker enrolled for a course in 1898, concentrated on romantic views of the north German moorland. Her own interests were increasingly ______ theirs: she traveled repeatedly to Paris, and her mature pictures are unsparing self-portraits and figures, among them the earliest nude self-portraits known to be by a woman painter.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: At odds with something means in conflict with it. The colony concentrated on “romantic views of the north German moorland,” while her mature pictures are “unsparing self-portraits and figures,” so her interests pulled against the colony’s.

A.why_wrong: Typical of something means representative of it. Her self-portraits and figures are set against the colony’s romantic landscapes, not offered as examples of them.

C.why_wrong: Secondary to something means less important than it. The text contrasts the two kinds of painting; it does not rank them.

D.why_wrong: Borrowed from something means taken over from it. The sentence says her interests diverged from the colony’s, and the examples given are of a different kind of picture.

sources.what: Paula Modersohn-Becker attended a course at the Worpswede artists' colony, which remained rooted in romanticized traditions of landscape while her own artistic interests shifted toward Paris; she is noted for many self-portraits, including nudes, and is recognized as the first known woman painter to paint nude self-portraits

items.notes: Subject: humanities (painting). Key letter B. Phrase options on one frame; contrast clue with the examples after the colon. Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): typical of absent; at odds with absent; secondary to absent; borrowed from absent. Key is not the longest option.

items.passage: The Chiricahua Apache fighter Lozen left no written testimony of her own. What is known of her, including her rides with the band led by her brother Victorio during the campaigns of 1879 to 1881, is largely ______ recollections that survivors such as James Kaywaykla published decades afterward, accounts crediting her with the power to sense where an enemy was.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Confined to something means limited to it. The text says Lozen “left no written testimony of her own,” so what is known of her comes almost entirely from the recollections survivors published long afterward.

A.why_wrong: Contrary to something means in conflict with it. The survivors’ accounts are the source of what is known about Lozen, not evidence against it.

B.why_wrong: Supplemented by something means added to by it. That would require some other body of evidence about Lozen for the recollections to fill out, but the text names none: she left no testimony of her own, and what is known rests “largely” on the later recollections.

D.why_wrong: Indifferent to something means unaffected by it. What is known of Lozen depends on these accounts rather than ignoring them.

sources.what: Lozen (c. 1840-1889), Chihenne Chiricahua Apache warrior and prophet, sister of Victorio; according to legends she could learn the movements of the enemy; the article's account of her in Victorio's War (1879-1881) rests on the recollections of James Kaywaykla, a child at the time (his In the Days of Victorio: Recollections of a Warm Springs Apache, ed. Eve Ball, 1970s, is cited across the related articles)

items.notes: Subject: history. Key letter C. Phrase options on one frame; the clue is the restatement in sentence 1 (almost nothing written down in her lifetime). Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): contrary to absent; supplemented by absent; confined to absent; indifferent to absent. Key is not the longest option.

fixes: opening premise 'Almost nothing the Chiricahua Apache fighter Lozen said was documented during her lifetime' is not on the source page: replaced by 'left no written testimony of her own' (not stated on the page either, but a safe inference: no writing by Lozen is known, and the article draws on others' recollections); 'furnished' to 'published' (Kaywaykla's recollections appeared in print in the 1970s); explanation and why_wrong for supplemented by rewritten to the new clue

items.passage: Painters before Guan Daosheng, who worked in ink under the early Yuan dynasty, ordinarily arranged a few bamboo branches flat against the front of the picture. In Bamboo Groves in Mist and Rain, attributed to her, the stems stand among neighboring thickets and half disappear into atmospheric haze: she presented the plant as an element of a ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A landscape is a stretch of scenery. The text says that in the painting attributed to her “the stems stand among neighboring thickets and half disappear into atmospheric haze,” which places the bamboo in a setting instead of flat at the front of the picture.

A.why_wrong: A procession is a line of people or things moving along. The thickets and haze described are scenery, not a file of anything.

B.why_wrong: A doctrine is a set of taught principles. The example describes what the painting looks like, not a body of teaching.

D.recipe: near miss: wrong kind of whole (CONNOT)
D.why_wrong: A collection is a gathered group of items. The bamboo is shown inside a scene with its own weather and distance, not as one of several objects assembled.

sources.what: Guan Daosheng (1262-1319) painted ink bamboo in the early Yuan dynasty; her greatest contribution to bamboo painting was her tendency to paint it as part of a landscape rather than as isolated branches pressed close to the picture plane, as in Bamboo Groves in Mist and Rain, attributed to her, where the bamboo grows among the thickets and is subject to the misty atmosphere around it

items.notes: Subject: humanities (painting). Key letter C. The example after the colon instantiates the abstract category in the blank, as in official easy B4 items. Raw freq.txt ranks: procession 3,521; doctrine 5,690; landscape 3,534; collection 4,203. Key is not the longest option.

items.passage: One can hardly ______ the versatility of the entertainer Valaida Snow. By the age of fifteen she had learned the cello, banjo, violin, mandolin, harp, accordion and saxophone, and on tour she sang and danced as well as playing the trumpet that earned her the nickname Little Louis, bestowed in tribute to Louis Armstrong.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To overstate something is to make it sound greater than it is. The text lists seven instruments Snow had learned by fifteen and adds that she sang and danced as well as playing the trumpet, so a claim about her versatility can hardly be too large.

B.why_wrong: To applaud something is to praise it. The sentence is about how large a claim her versatility will bear, not about whether praise is possible.

C.why_wrong: To itemize something is to list its parts one by one, which is what the text does; the text treats that as straightforward rather than hardly possible.

D.why_wrong: To understate something is to describe it as smaller than it is. Saying one can hardly understate her versatility would mean the seven instruments, the singing and the dancing made her range small.

sources.what: Valaida Snow (1904-1956) was an American jazz musician and entertainer who by the age of fifteen had learned cello, bass, banjo, violin, mandolin, harp, accordion, clarinet, trumpet and saxophone, also sang and danced, and was nicknamed “Little Louis” after Louis Armstrong

items.notes: Subject: humanities (music). Key letter A. Negated frame with the negator hardly in the blank's own sentence; the example list is the clue. The official frame It would be a mistake to ______ was dropped after check_rw found it in item 1.37. Raw freq.txt ranks: overstate absent; applaud 17,303; itemize absent; understate 74,502. Key is not the longest option.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Mary Hartwell Catherwood’s 1901 novel Lazarre. The narrator is traveling with his companion, Doctor Chantry, who has again quarreled with a stranger.

He hung his head in such a dejected manner that I felt ashamed of bringing his temperament to account: and told him I was certain no harm would come of it.

“I am not genial,” Doctor Chantry <u>owned</u>; “I wish I were. Now you are genial, Lazarre. People take to you. You attract them.”
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “owned” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Doctor Chantry says of himself, “I am not genial,” and adds, “I wish I were.” He is granting something unflattering about himself, so owned here means acknowledged.

A.why_wrong: Owned often means possessed, but what follows the verb is a statement he makes, not property he holds.

C.why_wrong: To own something can suggest having control of it, but Doctor Chantry is conceding a fault, not directing anything.

D.why_wrong: Boasted would mean he said it with pride. He hangs his head and wishes he were otherwise.

sources.what: Public-domain text of Mary Hartwell Catherwood, Lazarre (1901), Project Gutenberg eBook 15108; the sentences are copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter B. Common polysemous verb in a secondary sense, as in official easy M1 items; two distractors are other senses of own. Raw freq.txt ranks: Possessed 1,404; Admitted 1,700; Controlled 6,019; Boasted 9,444. Key is not the longest option.

items.passage:
The following text is from John Habberton’s 1877 short story “Mr. Putchett’s Love.” Mr. Putchett is spending the summer at a seaside resort.

A <u>stout</u> rope was stretched from a post on the shore to a buoy in deep water where it was anchored, and back and forth on this rope capered every day twenty or thirty hideously dressed but very happy people, among whom might always be seen Mr. Putchett with a child on his shoulder.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “stout” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The rope is “stretched from a post on the shore to a buoy in deep water” and holds twenty or thirty bathers who move along it every day. Stout here describes a rope strong enough for that.

B.why_wrong: Stout can describe a person of thickset build, but it is a rope that is described here.

C.why_wrong: Stout can mean brave, as in a stout defense. A rope has no courage; what matters is that it holds.

D.why_wrong: Rigid means stiff and unbending. The rope is stretched between a post and a buoy and bathers move along it, which calls for strength rather than stiffness.

sources.what: Public-domain text of John Habberton, Little Guzzy, and Other Stories (1877), the story “Mr. Putchett's Love”; Project Gutenberg eBook 67985; the sentence is copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter A. A common adjective fixed by its noun, the official easy pattern; two distractors are other senses of stout. Raw freq.txt ranks: Sturdy 6,198; Plump 7,205; Brave 1,264; Rigid 4,114. Key is the longest option.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Will N. Harben’s 1912 novel Paul Rundel. Hoag, who is on horseback, has been praising the boy Paul for standing up to a group of men.

No appreciation of these profuse compliments showed itself in the boy’s face. An angry retort trembled on his lips, and even this Hoag seemed to note and relish. His smile was unctuous; he <u>checked</u> his horse more firmly.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “checked” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Hoag is on horseback and wants to stay where the boy is, so he holds the animal back. Checking a horse “more firmly” means tightening the hold that keeps it from moving on.

A.why_wrong: To check something can mean to inspect it, but Hoag is sitting on the horse and keeping it in place while he talks.

B.why_wrong: To check can mean to tally, as in checking a list. There is nothing here to count, and “more firmly” describes a grip.

C.why_wrong: To check can mean to put a mark against something. A mark cannot be made more firmly on a horse that is being held in place.

sources.what: Public-domain text of Will N. Harben, Paul Rundel: A Novel (1912), Project Gutenberg eBook 50898; the sentences are copied exactly, with one sentence between the first and second omitted

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter D. Three distractors are other senses of check, as in official M1 items where every distractor is a real sense of the target. Raw freq.txt ranks (rarest content word): Examined 3,085; Counted 3,133; Marked 1,561; Reined in absent. Key is the longest option.

fixes: intro 'is from' to 'is adapted from', since a sentence between the first and second is omitted; text otherwise checked against Gutenberg 50898
